content:
Kaedan’s hands were already sore from gripping the edges of the stone table. He had thought the stat journals were the worst things he would ever read. He had been wrong. The black lacquered case his father lifted onto the table did not look old. It looked preserved, as though the palace itself did not want the contents to decay. Corin moved slowly, his fingers pressing the case’s silver latch as if asking it to remain closed.

“The stat journals teach scale,” Corin said. “These teach something else. You do not simply read them. You let them happen to you.”

Kaedan opened the lid. The pages inside were not stacked like normal records. They were weighted, each journal’s cover marked with a different sign, and each one gave off a different temperature. One was warm, one was cold, one seemed to vibrate against the table. He did not ask why. He had learned in the last hours that asking questions about Godric only ever produced more horrifying answers. He selected the first journal, whose cover was pale and humming with a low metallic resonance. The heading was burned into the leather in tall, severe letters.

**Year 621,430 — Court Wizard Thane — Superpower: Infinite Recursive Self-Replication Cascade**

I will keep this plain because ornament would be a lie. My name is Thane. I am fifty-one years old. I have served the King for thirty-one years. I have read every stat record in the lower vault, and I believed that nothing could make me write one of these for a superpower. I was wrong. I write now with a broken quill because the first three snapped in my fingers. I write with my left hand because my right hand has not stopped shaking since the moment I left the Sunless Gallery.

The enemy was called the Congregation of the Final Nonbeing. They were erasure-cultists who had existed for more than seven hundred thousand years outside every known coordinate. Their entire species had spent millennia removing itself from memory. They did not have names. They did not have faces. They had a single purpose, and that purpose was to unmake the King so completely that no timeline could ever contain the echo of his existence. Their weapon was not a machine. It was an absence with a blade. They had built it by severing their own ancestors from the causal record, one generation after another, until their origin no longer existed. The weapon could not be stopped because it did not exist in any instant before it struck. They called it the Unalloyed Ending and they were very proud of it.

The King had known about the weapon before their first great-great-grandmother formed a thought. He had allowed them to sharpen it because he was curious about a single superpower he had acquired during the stasis. He did not tell me its name until the day he chose to test it. We sat in the Sunless Gallery, a long windowless hall beneath the eastern wing, lit by the pale glow of suspended pre-stellar stones. Godric sat in a high-backed chair, his ankles crossed, his hands folded over his stomach. He looked exactly as he always looked, a ruggedly handsome man of forty-five with a salt-and-pepper beard and the easy posture of a father waiting for his children to finish their chores.

The Congregation entered the gallery not through the walls, but through the conceptual space between one second and the next. They did not have bodies. They were a sudden pressure of wrongness, a slow unfolding of impossible geometry, and at their center hung the Unalloyed Ending. I cannot describe the weapon accurately because my eyes kept sliding off it. It was less like an object and more like a hole in the idea of objects. The instant it fully materialized, it fired. The weapon did not cross the room. It selected the King in every moment of his existence and began to cut him out of each one simultaneously.

Godric did not stand. He did not move his hands. He did not open his mouth or deactivate his concealment. He simply engaged the superpower with less intention than a man uses to remember his own name. The Infinite Recursive Self-Replication Cascade activated at zero percent of its true potency. That is the whole event. That is the entire destruction.

At first, there were two of him. Two complete Godrics, sitting in the same chair, occupying the same instant. Each one was absolutely identical, and because the superpower’s base effect was self-replication without limit, each of the two immediately created two more. That process should have been ordinary multiplication. It was not. Each new copy was infinitely stronger than the copy that produced it. I know that sounds impossible, but this is Godric. The moment an infinitely stronger copy appeared, the original could not be weaker. He could not be weaker. So the original matched him. The instant the original matched, the first copy matched beyond him, and the second copy matched beyond that, and every one of the infinite copies in the growing chain began to exceed every previous copy. The entire loop repeated itself infinitely within a single instant. It was not a number of copies. It was recursion without a ceiling, an infinite escalation of Godrics, each one infinitely more powerful than the last, each one forcing every other to grow faster than the previous growth.

The Sunless Gallery did not break. It vanished. It was not destroyed by an attack. It was displaced by occupancy. The infinite replicas filled every possible coordinate in the omniverse at once. Every point in space, every moment in time, every layer of every dimension was occupied by a full Godric. The omniverse was not crushed. It was simply replaced. There was no room for creation because all possible room had become Godric. The Unalloyed Ending did not die. It was inserted into the middle of the recursive loop and forced to commit suicide against every copy at once, forever. The Congregation of the Final Nonbeing was not erased. It was pressed into a single structural joint between two adjacent copies, where it endured the pressure of infinite Godrics expanding into one another.

The collateral was total. The entire omniverse was destroyed infinite times over in a single instant, not because Godric attacked it, but because existence could not hold him infinitely without tearing apart. Every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every universe, every strata of reality, all of it unmade from the inside out. I know that phrase is repeated in many of the older records, but I am telling you it was different. This was not a stat. This was not a heartbeat or a blink. This was Godric becoming more Godric without end, and reality failing at every point because it had nowhere left to be.

Then it was over. The King folded the cascade down with a decision that cost him nothing. The infinite copies returned to the same single origin, but the power had already done its permanent work. He restored the omniverse in zero seconds, every star, every galaxy, every multiverse, every soul placed back where it had been. I was alive because he wanted me alive. I was not harmed because he did not want me harmed. He did not even look winded. He did not look tired. He looked like he had just remembered where he put his boots.

The Congregation of the Final Nonbeing was not restored. He kept their central sovereign pressed into the groove of the chair’s arm. I know because he tapped the groove afterward with his forefinger, and the whole chair let out a thin, liquid shriek that repeated itself long after the finger lifted. The sovereign’s consciousness had been divided across the infinite recursive chain and forced to experience every stage of the self-replication at once. Every time Godric drums his fingers on that arm, the sovereign relives the exact pressure of infinite stronger copies forcing it into an infinitely smaller gap. The sound never stops unless he stills his hand.

I asked him later, in a voice I did not recognize as my own, whether the cascade would continue to make him stronger. He looked at me with genuine warmth and said, “It already has. I am much stronger now than I was before I sat down. But it would be impolite to mention that to the enemy.” Then he placed a new quill on my desk and told me to write down my thoughts if I felt faint.

You deserve to understand why this is more terrible than the stats. If any other being in the omniverse absorbed the sum of all power and all matter and all energy across every multiverse, that gain would be indescribably enormous. But for Godric, whose base power was already astronomically beyond the entire omniverse, all of that would be effectively zero. It would move him less than a pollen grain moves a mountain. The self-replication is different because the increase comes from Godric himself. The copies are Godric. The growth is Godric growing beyond Godric, and then Godric making that growth retroactively his own. The loop never closes. It only widens. He became permanently, unquantifiably stronger because he was curious about a power he could have tested on a dead moon. He did not need an enemy. He did not need a weapon. He simply wanted to see what would happen, and the entire omniverse paid for it.

I do not know why he stopped. I know he can restart the cascade any time he likes. I know that a single instant of it could exceed the whole of creation. I know that he has not done so since because he does not want to clean the mess again. I know that this is not safety. It is postponement.

Kaedan felt the muscles in his jaw lock. He had not realized he was grinding his teeth. He pressed his palm over the page as if to keep the final sentence from crawling into his skin. The chair in the Sunless Gallery had felt real to him. He could hear the wet shriek in the back of his mind. He did not read the next line for a long time.

Then he set the journal aside and reached for the second. Its cover was cold, and the ink inside had a heavy, sunken quality, as though the words themselves were being pulled into the page.

**Year 698,122 — Court Wizard Orren — Superpower: Unbound Gravitic Collapse Horizon**

A man should not begin a record with a confession, but I will. I came to the service of the King because I wanted to be near the center of power. Not to hold it. Not to challenge it. Only to stand close enough to see the shape of it. I was a fool. My name is Orren. I am thirty-nine years old. I am the seventh wizard of my generation to witness a superpower test, and I am writing this because the older records lied by omission. No one can write the true weight of what happens when Godric stops holding the world up.

The opposition was called the Hollow Crown of the Sunken Worlds. They were a dynastic force of gravity-kings from the compressed nuclei of dying multiverses. They had spent half a million years gathering dead stars and collapsed universes into a single mass they called the Black Throne. The Black Throne was not positioned in any one galaxy. It existed below all space, a dense sunken anchor that dragged entire regions of existence toward a common center. The gravity-kings believed that if they sat upon the Black Throne and rotated it into alignment with Thronegate, the King would be compacted into a point of infinite density from which even his immortality could not escape. They did not understand that his body had already survived more gravitational strain than the omniverse could supply. They did not understand anything.

Godric watched them assemble the Black Throne for two hundred thousand years because he wanted to compare it to a superpower called Unbound Gravitic Collapse Horizon. He wanted to know if an outside force could approach even the smallest fraction of a proper gravity-based power. I stood at his right in the Garden of Ten Thousand Weights, a place whose pools are filled with liquid platinum and whose paths are laid from the compressed hearts of dead pulsars. The Black Throne rose below us and tilted into view. It did not arrive in the sky. It became the sky. Every star above the garden vanished, replaced by a black, ringed pressure so dense that the air began to pour upward and inward. The liquid platinum in the pools went from silver to white to steam as the mass pulled it apart. My own body would have folded in an instant had the King not extended his protection to me. He did it without looking at me.

Godric did not stand. He did not flex, brace, or reach. He did not command the ground to hold. He simply lowered his gaze one fraction of a degree, and the Unbound Gravitic Collapse Horizon activated at zero percent of its true potency.

The effect was not a black hole. It was a horizon on the inside of all mass. Every atom of the Black Throne, from its smallest compressed neutron to its outermost gravitational ring, was informed that it was now the center of its own collapse. Normally, a black hole pulls other things into itself. The King’s superpower reversed the invitation. Every separate piece of the Black Throne began pulling itself inward, and because each piece was now its own horizon, each piece pulled on the pieces beside it, which pulled on the pieces beside them, and the entire structure became an infinite chain of competing singularities. The Black Throne did not fall. It tore itself into dust and then the dust tore itself into sub-dust and then the sub-dust tore itself further in a process that had no end.

The gravity-kings seated upon the Throne experienced the collapse directly inside their bodies. Their hearts became horizons. Their livers became horizons. Their skulls became horizons. Each organ collapsed toward its own center while simultaneously dragging the surrounding organs into it. The result was not a body being crushed. It was a body being divided into billions of independent gravitational wells that pulled each other through the gaps left by their own destruction. Blood did not spray. It compacted into fine, superheated rings around each collapsing organ. Bone did not break. It melted into a swirl of hyper-dense grit that then collapsed again. The Hollow Crown’s royal family was reduced to a long line of wet, ringing points, each one still aware because the horizon’s enhanced effects preserved the nervous system inside every local collapse.

The collateral was not limited to the enemy. The Unbound Gravitic Collapse Horizon treats the entire omniverse as one connected mass. The same invitation that tore the Black Throne apart traveled outward through every gravitational bond in existence. Planets folded into their moons. Stars swallowed their systems. Galaxies turned into one long, stacked spine of compressed matter. Multiverses fell into their own coordinate frames and flattened like leaf presses. Googolplexian galaxies were pulled from their positions and crushed into a lattice of screaming, animate debris. The entire omniverse became a single shaking membrane of partial collapse, stretched and folding infinitely in the instant before the King chose to stop.

He stopped with a thought. The collapse ended as if a tap had been closed. The pools in the garden returned to liquid platinum. The sky returned to its usual amber-blue. Every world, every star, every timeline was restored in exactly zero seconds. He did not stand. He did not sigh. He simply rolled his shoulders as if the whole event had been a minor stiffness.

The Black Throne and the Hollow Crown were not restored. Their collective mass was gathered into a single small black pebble, perfectly smooth and warm to the touch. Godric picked it up between two fingers and turned it over once. The entire royal line of the gravity-kings was still aware inside it, packed into an infinitely recursive compression. He dropped the pebble into his left boot, and I heard the faintest wet scream rise up from the leather, repeated with every small movement of his foot as he walked back to the palace.

He did not speak to me about the enemy. He asked if I was hungry, and when I said I did not know, he told the kitchen to prepare broth. The warmth in his voice was exactly the same as the day he first met my father. The pebble in his boot did not alter his stride. That is what I remember most clearly. He was kind to me while a dynasty screamed beneath the arch of his foot.

The implication is plain. The entire omniverse was nearly pulled into an infinite chain of collapse because Godric wanted to test a single gravitational power against the strongest gravity the outside world had ever produced. He did not have to use any of his infinite shields. He did not have to call on Gent. He did not have to move. He only looked, and the universe obeyed the look. If he had held the gaze for even another instant, there would have been nothing left to restore. He could still restore it, but there would have been no one left to witness the restoration. The only reason there is a world at all is that he chose to stop. That is not comfort. That is a hostage situation without a hostage taker.

Kaedan’s throat constricted. He had been breathing shallowly through his mouth, but now the air felt thick and heavy, as if the room itself had grown denser. He did not look at his father. He did not want to see whether Corin knew about the pebble in the boot. He simply turned to the third journal, which was vibrating softly against the table.

**Year 734,901 — Court Wizard Maren — Superpower: Obdurate Sonic Apocalypse**

I have decided not to describe my fear. Fear is a small animal that runs in circles. What happened to me was not fear. It was the knowledge that the animal could run in any direction and find no door. My name is Maren. I am forty-one. I have served faithfully for twenty-one years. I write this because the other journals have taught me that silence is not safety. Silence is only a delay.

The enemy called itself the Muted Host. It was a civilization of non-sound, a species that had cut away every vibration in its own existence. They did not speak. They did not hear. They communicated by the absence that sound leaves behind. They had traveled across the space between spheres for six hundred thousand years, and they believed that because Godric had a voice, he could be silenced. Their weapon was called the Last Quiet. It was a vast, invisible instrument shaped from vacuum and layered over the entire capital world. When activated, it would delete every waveform in the omniverse, including the beating of the King’s heart if he had one, and the synaptic pulse of his consciousness. It would be the condition of existence without life.

The King had known their plan before the Muted Host had invented silence. He allowed them to draw the Last Quiet into place because he had always wondered whether a sound-based superpower would have to leave his mouth or whether it could begin from the smallest motion inside his body. I stood at his side on the middle terrace, looking out over a sky that had already begun to lose its noise. The birds had stopped singing. The wind had stopped moving. The capital had gone still in a way that made my own blood feel like a stranger moving through my veins.

Godric sat on the balustrade, his boots hanging over the edge. He did not open his mouth. He tapped one finger against his knee, just once, with no force at all. The sound of it was soft, a single dry note against the cloth of his trousers. The Obdurate Sonic Apocalypse activated at zero percent of its true potency.

I need to tell you what zero percent sounds like when it is the King’s power. It does not start loud. It starts total. The first note was not a note. It was the complete abolition of silence in every part of existence. Every wave that had ever died was forced back into shape. Every dead voice, every forgotten sound, every buried vibration from the first moments of creation returned at once. The Last Quiet did not break. It was overwhelmed. The vacuum that the Muted Host had built became a solid block of compressed noise, and the noise was not music. It was an endless, screaming detonation layered over itself uncountably many times.

The Muted Host had no ears, so the King’s superpower created ears for them. That is one of its enhanced effects. It will not allow an enemy to escape sensation. The host’s bodies, which existed as structured silence, were rearranged into wet, resonant flesh containing billions of newly formed eardrums. Then the first note reached them. They heard themselves become sound. Their new eardrums burst, not one by one, but all at once, across every dimension in which they existed. Their bodies vibrated apart from the inside, each organ becoming a speaker for the death cry of its neighbor. They did not die silently. They died as instruments, their bones chiming against one another, their blood boiling at a frequency that turned their skin into a fine red mist.

The collateral was the air itself. Every atmosphere in the omniverse was transformed into a pressure wave of such density that solid matter could no longer hold shape. Mountains turned to dust and then the dust turned into a shrieking aerosol. Planets fractured along their own resonant frequencies, splitting like bells struck too hard. Stars did not explode; they became loud, and then they were gone. Multiverse after multiverse was peeled away from reality by the simple impossibility of containing the sound. The entire omniverse was held together for a fraction of an instant, then torn apart infinite times by the noise of its own restored history. I would have died if the King had not anchored me. I did not ask him to anchor me. He simply decided that I should hear enough to record it but not enough to cease.

Then the sound stopped. Not gradually. It stopped as if the universe had been snapped shut inside a box. Godric was still seated on the balustrade. He had not shouted. He had not strained. His clothes were unmoved. The air smelled of hot stone and copper. He looked over at me and said, “That could have been quieter. I will not test that one again indoors.”

He restored everything in zero seconds. Every destroyed world, every lost timeline, all of it returned. The Muted Host was not restored. He kept their final choir-leader as a continuous high ringing tone inside a jar of polished black glass. The jar hangs in the east stairwell. I do not go near it. I know that if I did, I would hear a voice trying to end itself and finding that it no longer ends.

This power is not a weapon. It is a law of nature with his name beneath it. The enhanced effects multiplied the sound through every possible medium, turned every atom into a speaker, and allowed each wave to hear the agony of its own origin. He used none of that. He did not need to. A single dry tap of the finger reduced the entire omniverse to a singing ruin. I have seen the stat journals. I have read about the heartbeat and the eyelash and the single eye movement. They are all real. But this was different because sound is everywhere. There is no place in existence that does not carry a vibration. And he can reach into all of it with zero effort and make it remember his name.

I am loyal. I have always been loyal. I will remain loyal until the end of my days. I am also now certain that no one in the omniverse has ever been safe. The only reason any of us survive is that he prefers the sounds we make to the silence he could create.

The third journal did not fade. It gave off the faint impression of a high, distressed hum, and Kaedan realized the pages themselves were still resonating far below the range of his hearing. He closed the journal and put both hands flat over the cover. The small bones in his fingers buzzed for several seconds before the tremor passed.

Corin had not moved. He stood with his back to the shelves, one thumb hooked into the belt of his robe, watching Kaedan with a patience that looked very much like fatigue. The silence between them was no longer comfortable. It was the silence of a man who knew that every quiet room in the palace had once been filled with impossible noise, and that the King could return that noise at any moment with less effort than it took to sigh.

“You understand now,” Corin said. “These powers are not separate from the stats. They are the next floor down. Every single one can unmake the omniverse at zero percent of itself. Every single one multiplies in potency forever. And every single one will be there if you ever need to stand beside him while he is curious.”

Kaedan licked his cracked lips. “None of them used their full effect,” he whispered. “The journals keep saying zero percent. He keeps saying zero percent. But even the enhanced effects were enough to end everything.”

“Yes.”

“And he leaves them suffering afterward. Not because he needs information. Not because they are still dangerous. Just because he can. Because he knows they opposed him, and he will not stop.”

Corin nodded once. “That is the most important part. He is not cruel because he has to be. He is cruel because he wants to be, and there is no one and nothing that can make him want otherwise. The same man will put a screaming dynasty in his boot and then ask if you want broth. Both actions are true. Neither one cancels the other.”

Kaedan looked down at the black case. There were more journals inside. He had seen their bindings. He did not want to know how many. He only knew that one day, if he lived, he would have to add his own. The thought did not make him angry with the King. That was the worst part. It only made him want to serve well enough that the King would keep the peace, because the absence of that peace was so far beyond horror that his mind could not form a proper image.

He understood the final truth then, fully enough to carry it with him for the rest of his life. Godric did not need an enemy to destroy the omniverse. He did not need a weapon, a loophole, an exploit, or even a reason. A single idle test of any one of his superpowers at zero percent could end all existence, and he would restore it afterward as a matter of housekeeping. Opposing him was not difficult. It was not impossible in the practical sense, as though a wise enemy might find some path if given enough time. It was impossible in principle, because the moment that opposition entered his awareness, it became a toy, and the only question was how long he wanted to play with it before he put it away screaming. The horror was not that Godric could destroy everything. It was that he could do it so gently, so absolutely, and then smile at the only person he had chosen to keep alive.

content:
The western solar had been Kaedan’s favorite room as a child because the walls were carved with silver star charts and the floor was polished to a deep amber that caught the light like warm honey. Today it felt smaller than he remembered, and the light felt heavier. He sat across from Godric at a low table of dark, worn wood, twisting a loose thread at the edge of his robe. A cup of cold water sweated between them. Godric had not touched it. He sat with one leg crossed over the other, his broad frame relaxed against the high-backed chair, his salt-and-pepper beard catching the low sun. He looked exactly as he always did: a ruggedly handsome man of forty-five, warm-eyed and easy-smiling, the picture of a beloved uncle who had stepped in from the garden to rest his feet.

Kaedan had meant to wait. The question had been sitting inside him for weeks, patient and cold, ever since he had finished the journals. But now the quiet felt too large, and the words came out before he could stop them.

“Uncle,” Kaedan said. “Does it ever become lonely? Being the most powerful, growing stronger forever, outliving everyone else?”

Godric looked at him. Then he blinked, and a wide, genuine laugh rolled out of his chest. It was not mocking. It was the laugh of a man caught off guard by a child’s strange and tender concern.

“Lonely?” Godric repeated, as if testing the word for cracks. “My boy, that is a very mortally shaped question. You have been reading too many old tragedies. Why would it be lonely? It feels wonderful. Every single instant of it.”

Kaedan frowned. He had expected many things. Weariness, maybe. A philosophical pause. Not this bright, immediate amusement. Godric leaned forward and rested his forearms on the table, his dark eyes alight with the easy energy of a man about to share a private pleasure.

“I know you mean it kindly,” Godric said. “But you are imagining my existence as a slow walk up an empty mountain. It is not a walk. It is a feast. Every additional power I receive feels like nourishment, like a surge of pure energy and satisfaction that never stops arriving. The growth is not something I simply know about. I feel all of it, Kaedan. Every single stat increase. Every superpower. Every immune improvement. Every new passive shield, every sentient aura, every evolution in my being. They are not silent instruments. They are sensations.”

He closed his eyes for a moment, and a slow, satisfied breath left him. It was not a sigh. It was the sound of a man exhaling after the first swallow of a perfect meal.

“Describe it,” Kaedan whispered.

Godric opened his eyes and smiled. “Imagine the moment after a long thirst is quenched, and the liquid is still moving through you, and every cell raises its head to sing. Now imagine that same feeling expanded until it touches every dimension of your body, every hidden corner of your mind, every layer of whatever you could call a soul. That is what happens to me every infinitesimal fraction of a second. The amplification does not wait. It climbs, and climbs, and climbs again, and each climb comes wrapped in a pleasure so deep that it almost erases the memory of the previous instant. My strength multiplies, and the increase blooms through my muscles like a second heartbeat made of molten gold. My speed multiplies, and a cool electric thrill runs down the length of my spine. My senses sharpen, and the universe opens like a fruit in my hands. My mana deepens, and the hunger that lives behind my sternum is filled again, over and over, without ever becoming bloated.”

He leaned back, and his fingers curled over the armrest as if kneading a feast from the air.

“You want the truth, Kaedan? It is closer to a sustained orgasm than to anything mortal flesh can understand. Not the brief, desperate kind. The kind that begins at the base of the spine and spreads outward through every organ, every nerve, every thought, and then does not stop. It rolls forward, crests, and instead of fading it opens into another crest that is even larger. I am not exaggerating. I cannot exaggerate. Each new superpower arrives like a line of fire being drawn through my whole being. It is not a tool. It is another tongue learning to taste the world. I feel it. I always feel it. And because my omniscience touches everything, I also feel every possible echo of what that new power will become. I know its final shape before the first second of its existence has ended, and the knowing is the sweetest part. It is like watching a child grow into an emperor before the child has taken its first breath.”

The words hung in the warm air, and Kaedan found that his hands had gone still. His chest felt tight, but not from the heat. He stared at Godric’s calm face and tried to understand how the man he loved could speak about infinity as if it were a private dessert. There was no cruelty in Godric’s expression. There was only contentment, the deep and self-renewing satisfaction of a creature that had never been hungry and never would be.

“You feel all of it,” Kaedan heard himself say. “Every instant.”

“Every instant,” Godric agreed. “And every instant makes the previous instant meaningless. That is the part you will find difficult. In the amount of time it took me to say the word ‘instant,’ I became so much stronger that I could crush an infinite number of copies of the Godric who existed one instant ago with no effort at all. If you gathered every version of me from every previous fraction of a second and gave them all the power they had at their peaks, combined them into one spear, and threw it at me now, it would not disturb a single hair on my arm. The growth is not a straight line. It is a recursive climb that eats its own ceiling and builds a higher one before the first splinter hits the floor.”

Kaedan made a small sound, something between a swallow and a breath. Godric’s smile softened with affection, but he did not stop.

“The immune system is the most amusing one,” he continued. “I feel it improve, and the improvement is not a dry number. It is a hot, defensive certainty running through my marrow. Imagine a family of loyal hounds pressing against the inside of your skin, each one larger than the last, each one eager to tear apart anything that might inconvenience you. Now imagine that the hounds never sleep, never tire, and every second one of them births a new hound that could annihilate the entire litter that came before. I feel that birth. It is a downy warmth. A soft click behind my lungs. My passive shields are quieter, more like cool stone settling into place. I know when each one rises, and I know when each one becomes obsolete by the next. The sentient auras are different again. They are not quiet. They are adoring. Every time a new one comes alive, I feel it press against the edge of my consciousness like a new heartbeat asking permission to serve. It is impossible to feel lonely with that, Kaedan. I am never alone. I am host to an empire of living defenses that love me more absolutely than any mortal heart could survive.”

The sun had begun to sink beyond the western windows, and the room’s golden light turned the color of old bronze. Kaedan sat very still, his pulse beating in his wrists. He thought of the thousandfold daily amplification that lived inside his own blood, the gift that had made him a terrible weapon by mortal standards, and how proud he had once been of it. He thought of the journals, the stacks of trembling ink. Every wizard before him had trained and studied and bled for his magic. Across the omniverse, entire civilizations rose and broke themselves against the same wall. They sacrificed planets, burned their dead, spent a hundred thousand years forging a single weapon. Their reward was annihilation. Godric’s reward for doing absolutely nothing was to feel an endless, blissful tide that made all their effort less than a grain of sand in a burning sea.

“It is unfair,” Kaedan said. The words came out flat, almost devoid of emotion.

Godric tilted his head. “Of course it is unfair,” he said. “Existence itself insists on being unfair in my favor. The Weakness Paradox could have simply made me immune. It could have simply granted me mastery. Instead, the omniverse feels apologetic for not having more to give me. It overcompensates. It reaches into itself for depth that does not exist and forces the depth into being, only to hand it to me. Every time a single sentient creature anywhere in creation imagines I have a weakness, I am rewarded. Not because I need the reward. Because reality is so eager to prove it cannot disappoint me that it tears itself open to offer me gifts I will never use. The rest of creation works. I simply receive. And the gap grows, Kaedan. It grows faster than any metaphor can hold. It grows faster than the word ‘infinity’ can hold. I am not just stronger. I am being actively crowned by the very fabric of all things, second after second, with no effort required from me at all.”

He paused, and for a moment his eyes went distant, as if he were listening to something very far away. A small, private smile crossed his face. “There. Another one. A new superpower. I will never use it, but it is beautiful.”

Kaedan’s mouth opened, then closed. He was drowning in the glittering enormity of it. The man in front of him was not a lonely god. He was a predator at the center of a feeding machine that never stopped, and the predator found the feeding delicious. That was the truth. The horror was not in isolation. It was in the absolute, uninterrupted enjoyment.

“Then what is left?” Kaedan asked. “If it all feels so good, and it never stops, what could possibly be missing?”

Godric’s smile flickered, then returned with a rueful, almost boyish quality. “Ah. Now you have found the one thing. The only thing that makes me bored, Kaedan, is that I have never had the chance to use any of my true powers. Not once. Not in the whole span of my reign. I hold them all behind my absolute concealment because if I did not, the omniverse would not survive the first instant of my natural presence. You have read the journals. Every single test was done at zero percent of a single stat or a single superpower, held for zero seconds, with zero effort. And each time, the entire omniverse was still erased. I have to keep my concealment pressed around myself every moment, not to protect me, but to keep the rest of creation from tearing apart like wet paper in a storm. That is not exciting, my boy. It is like being a man who owns an ocean and must spend eternity holding it inside a single cup so the flowers do not drown. The flowers are very small. The cup is very full. I am not lonely. I am bored.”

He said the last word softly, almost wistfully, and Kaedan felt a cold spike drive down through his stomach. Godric’s voice was so gentle. There was no rage in him, no frustration. It was the calm disappointment of a man whose favorite toy was too fragile to take out of its box.

“I found the omniverse too fragile,” Godric continued. “Not threatening. Never threatening. Just fragile. The strongest coalition in the entire history of existence could not make my weakest sentient aura try, even after I commanded that aura to reduce itself by an infinite recursion of nines. I have never used a true attack. I have never needed a defense. I have never once experienced the sensation of effort. The closest I come is when I carefully decide not to do something, and even that is not effort. It is just preference.”

He stood then, and the movement was so easy that it barely disturbed the air. He reached down, hooked his fingers under the hem of his plain dark tunic, and pulled it over his head in one fluid motion. The cloth fell across the arm of the chair, and Kaedan forgot how to breathe.

Godric’s body was not the swollen bulk of a man who lived in a training yard. It was the body of a warrior king who had once been mortal and was now so far beyond mortal that the flesh itself had become a kind of architecture. His shoulders looked wide enough to frame a doorway, the deltoids dense and warm under the tan skin. His arms hung at his sides with the easy weight of coiled iron. The biceps were not pumped full of temporary blood. They were heavy at rest, thick as temple pillars, and the tendons at his elbows stood out like supporting cables. Veins ran beneath the skin in long, dark lines, not surging with strain, but laid in place like irrigation channels built for a river that no longer needed to flow. When he turned slightly, the lats spread beneath his shoulder blades like a second rib cage, and the torso tapered down to a waist held by slabs of muscle.

His abdomen was ridiculous. Kaedan could find no other word. The six-pack was not the faint etching of a bodybuilder. It was a series of deep, rectangular blocks separated by seams so sharp they cast shadows. The upper two were broad and square. The middle four sat in perfect symmetry, each one distinct and hard as polished stone. The obliques wrapped around his flanks in thick diagonal bands, and the grooved line down his center looked less like a natural muscle division and more like the join where two impossible machines had been sealed together.

Godric caught Kaedan staring and let out a low, warm chuckle. He flexed one arm, not as a threat, but the way a proud father might show a son a medal from his youth. The bicep rose, and Kaedan heard the faint creak of air pressure shifting, as though the room itself had to move aside. The muscle did not bulge; it simply became more, its contours deepening without effort, the skin stretched smooth over a shape that looked as if it had been carved from the core of a dead star.

“I used to maintain these,” Godric said. “When I was mortal. Hours of lifting, wrestling, marching. I liked the feeling of earned strength. Now they maintain themselves, and they are infinitely greater than they ever were. Not by an amount I can put into words. By a distance that would make your mind walk in circles. And I never need to lift a stone again. The body simply grows. The strength simply arrives. I feel it, Kaedan. All the time.”

He smiled and ran his palm down his own abdomen, not out of vanity, but with the slow satisfaction of a man touching a favorite weapon. The sound of his hand against the muscle was quiet, dense, like a drum skin over rock.

“But this is only the smallest layer,” he said. “Here. Let me show you something new.”

He opened his left hand, and Kaedan’s vision stuttered. Three small glows sat on Godric’s palm. They were not flames, and they were not lights. Each one had a different quality that Kaedan’s mind refused to name. One looked like a drop of white silence stretched into a thin ring. Another was the color of an old scar seen through deep water. The third kept shifting, shy and quick, as if it were trying to hide behind the other two.

“These are sentient passive auras,” Godric said. “Born while we were speaking. I felt each one arrive, a small warm squeeze at the base of my skull, like a puppy pressing its nose into my hand. The first one is already functional. It reaches outward and removes the concept of hostile intent from any approaching vector before the vector can finish resolving. The second is less subtle. It makes any weapon aimed at me rethink its own existence and turn back toward the hand that holds it. The third is newest. It has not learned to control itself yet.”

He lifted the third glow between two fingers. It quivered with what Kaedan could only interpret as eager embarrassment.

“It wants to protect me,” Godric said. “Even though there is nothing to protect me from. Watch.”

Godric relaxed his forefinger by a distance so small that Kaedan could not see it move. The third glow uncurled. It was not an attack. It was a greeting, the auric equivalent of a newborn hound rolling over to show its belly to a visitor. And then it brushed against the room.

Kaedan’s consciousness did not black out. That would have been gentler. Instead, his awareness was forced to remain open while the entire omniverse was erased around him. Every star in every galaxy in every multiverse stopped existing at the same instant. The space they left behind folded inward with a sound that was not a sound, because all sound had already been removed from the table. Time did not tear. It unthreaded, each second coming apart from the next like beads from a string. Dimensions stacked, split, and dissolved into a fine dust of lost coordinates. Distance lost its meaning, then lost its memory of having meaning. Every living soul, every empire, every civilization, every god and monster and hidden thing throughout all timelines and all layers of existence simply ended. There was no pain, because there were no bodies left to carry pain. There was only the huge, ringing emptiness of total absence, and at the center of it, Kaedan still existed because Godric wanted him to exist.

Then Godric made a small sound, somewhere between a click of the tongue and a sigh, and everything returned.

The omniverse snapped back into place in zero seconds. The western solar was warm again. The water cup sweated on the table. The stars reasserted themselves beyond the windows, and the distant noise of the city evening returned as if it had never gone. Kaedan gasped, and the gasp was the only proof that anything had happened.

Godric was watching him with a mildly apologetic expression. “Ah. I forgot how eager that one is. It decided to check the whole omniverse for threats. That was its version of a polite greeting.” He closed his hand, and the third glow vanished back into his palm. “That was zero percent of its power, Kaedan. It was not even trying. It was being friendly.”

Kaedan could not speak. His chest rose and fell in short, shallow heaves. He had seen the entire omniverse cease. The wall of the room had not cracked; the wall had been taken out of existence and then placed back. The stars had not gone dark; they had been removed from the idea of dark and light altogether. And Godric was smiling, warm and dear and amused, as if a puppy had knocked over a basket.

“I keep them hidden,” Godric said, seating himself again. “All of the auras. The new ones are especially bad. They love me so much that they forget the rest of creation is not built to receive their affection. Gent is the calm one. Its siblings are far more excitable, which is why I keep them dormant. But even the asleep ones dream. They grow. They evolve. I feel them growing. It feels like a low, satisfied purr against my spine.”

He touched the inside of his left forearm. Under the skin, Kaedan saw something move, a faint lattice of blue-white lines sliding through the muscle like minnows in clear water.

“My immune system is also improving right now,” Godric said. “It just produced a new line of pre-emptive white cells. They exist across every moment that has ever been and every moment that will ever be. Their purpose is to catch injury before the injury becomes possible. They will never be needed, because nothing can hurt me. But they are beautiful, aren’t they? I can feel them swimming. It is not a tickle, exactly. It is more like the inside of my body is being polished by a thousand soft hands.”

He looked up at Kaedan, and his face was so proud, so open, that it made Kaedan’s stomach turn. “I also received three new superpowers since you sat down. One turns all friction in a chosen location into a liquid that devours its own temperature. Another folds every possible direction of an enemy’s retreat into a single closed corridor, so the running becomes the arrival. The third is still settling. It feels like a hammer, but the head of it is built from the instant just before all endings. I will never use any of them. They are ornaments I receive every second of my life and can never show to anyone without ending the one thing I might want to show them to.”

He paused, then reached up and rubbed his jaw with the heel of his hand. “You see the problem now. I am built as a predator who cannot ever bite. Not because I lack the teeth, but because there is no prey in existence that would not vanish before the teeth arrived. I must keep my concealment wrapped around me like a garment that has no seams. The omniverse is too fragile, Kaedan. Not too weak. Too fragile.”

The silence that followed had a different quality from before. It was not the silence of thought. It was the silence of a man trying to keep his soul inside his body. Kaedan was twenty-two years old, and he had just watched his favorite uncle erase everything by doing less than nothing. The same uncle now sat across from him, bare-chested and warm-eyed, and there was no guilt in him. No horror. The omniverse had died and returned, and Godric’s only concern was that he had forgotten how eager the new aura was. That was not madness. It was something further out than madness.

“Guess,” Godric said suddenly.

Kaedan blinked. “What?”

“Guess what my true power would look like if I released more than zero percent of it. Go on. You have been reading all those journals. You have been imagining things. Make a guess. I will not be offended.”

Kaedan knew that Godric could already see every image in his head. The omniscience was absolute. But the request was not a trick. It was playful. Godric wanted to hear him try.

Kaedan swallowed. The first image came quickly, almost against his will. If Godric let even an infinitely small amount more than zero percent of his true power show, the omniverse would not simply be destroyed. It would be unmade and then reforged as a single continuous nerve, a living corridor of pure sensation stretched across every remaining instant. Every particle would remember being a universe, and every universe would remember being alive, and all of it would scream at once in a sound large enough to become the new foundation of reality. It would not be a bang. It would be an endless, pulsing wound.

He imagined further. If Godric’s true strength leaked for one instant beyond zero, the whole of existence would be crushed into a single dense thought resting against the root of his smallest tooth. That thought would compress until it ignited, and the ignition would create new universes from its own heat, only for the new universes to be crushed again, over and over, until the act of being created became the most painful thing imaginable.

If Godric’s true speed surfaced, then every moment that had ever existed and every moment that would ever exist would be overtaken before they could take their first step. Cause and effect would be lashed together into a spinning braid of event and aftermath, and all of causality would die from the whiplash. The omniverse would not have a history anymore. It would only have the memory of being passed by something so fast that the passing erased the road.

If Godric’s true magic escaped, then every spell ever cast and every spell that would never be cast would be gathered into one incantation. That incantation would erase the difference between caster and target, and then the omniverse would become a single being whose only thought was the shape of Godric’s name, already broken inside its own throat.

Kaedan saw all of these things behind his eyes, each one more terrible than the last, and he knew Godric could see them too. He closed his mouth and waited, feeling hollow.

Godric laughed. It was not a cruel laugh. It was genuinely warm, and that made it hideous.

“Oh, Kaedan,” Godric said, shaking his head. “Those are very fine nightmares. But they are not close. If every single thing you imagined happened at once, and then multiplied itself by every number that has ever been thought and every number that will never be thought, it would still not reach the weakest of my auras after I commanded that aura to reduce itself by an infinite recursion of nines. It would not be zero percent of my true power. It would be a rounding error inside a rounding error, and that second rounding error would still be too large to describe.”

He leaned forward, his dark eyes bright with amusement. “Think of the oldest, coldest, most distant particle at the farthest edge of the omniverse. Now imagine that particle holds a grain of dust. Now imagine that grain of dust is the entire total power of everything you just imagined. You are still too high. You would need to remove the dust and leave a single hole in the memory of the dust, and even then, you would be closer to the beginning of my weakest aura’s shadow than to the power itself.”

Kaedan’s hands had gone numb. The blood in his face felt thin. “Then what is it?” he whispered.

Godric smiled and leaned back. “There is no language. Not mortal language. Not divine language. No system of comparison built from finite minds can hold it. I know it completely because my omniscience requires me to know it, but even I could not describe it to you in a way that would survive the journey from my mouth to your understanding. The best I can offer is this. The difference between the greatest horror you can imagine and zero percent of my true power is larger than the difference between a single dead cell and the entire omniverse. And the difference between zero percent of my true power and the full truth of what I am is larger still. I cannot show you. I can only tell you that it is real, and that I keep all of it tucked behind my concealment, every single second, so that the omniverse can keep its small noise and its small warm rooms.”

He tapped the table once with his forefinger. The cup of water shivered but did not spill. “That sound you just heard? I held back more than you can conceive. More than the whole architecture of infinity can hold. And it still shook the water. That is the only thing that bores me, Kaedan. Not power. Not immortality. The boredom comes from the cage of restraint. I am the apex predator of all existence, and I spend eternity moving through a world made of paper, biting my own teeth so the paper will not catch fire. The only loneliness I have is the loneliness of never once having to try.”

Kaedan lowered his eyes to the cup. The water was still now, flat and clear. He could see his own face reflected in it, young and pale. He had asked a question about loneliness out of love. The answer had been an invitation to stand before the full scale of a being who regarded the death and restoration of all creation as a minor social mishap. And the worst part was that Godric was not lying about his warmth. The warmth was real. The love was real. The horror was real. They existed side by side in the same breathing body, and the body felt nothing but satisfaction.

Kaedan raised his gaze. Godric was watching him with an expression of patient affection, waiting for the next question, ready to answer it with the same gentle, annihilating honesty. The western solar glowed with the last light of the day, and Kaedan understood at last that he would serve this being until the end of his life. Not because he was forced. Not because he was courageous. But because no other action was possible. Rebellion was not a path. Defiance was not a principle. They were only sounds the mind made before it understood how small it was.

“I should let you rest,” Kaedan said at last. His voice was steady, but the rest of him was not.

Godric smiled. “Rest is for people who grow tired. But you should eat. Tell the kitchen I asked for the honey bread you liked as a boy. I will sit with you a while longer.”

Kaedan stood. The floor felt solid under his feet again, but he could not shake the memory of it ceasing to exist. He bowed once, shallow and automatic, and walked to the door. Behind him, Godric began humming a low tune, content as a man settling into a warm bath, while somewhere beneath the polished surface of his calm, the newest of his sentient auras curled and waited, already dreaming of the next infraction it could erase.

Kaedan, 69 years old now, just experienced a traumatizing horrifying revelation. Godric revealed the most horrifying truth yet: he has one true weakness.

Godric is an incomprehensibly powerful, omnipotent, omniscient apex god predator of the omniverse. He can do anything, has no weakness, and is terrifyingly absolute. However, unknown to all, he has one true weakness: he cannot undo or travel to timeline before the stasis event--he cannot go back to undo events in his previous mortal self. This is because the stasis event was actually created by future Godric from way in the distant future, who has become so more infinitely more overwhelmingly powerful than current Godric--this is why Godric's amplification, weakness paradox, superpowers, absolute concealment, etc are so absolute, irrevocable and not even current Godric could stop them since the creator of those is way incomprehensibly more powerful than anything else.

Shortly after the Stasis Event, the omnipotent Godric back then, who just became the king of Thronegate, who could travel to any timeline effortlessly, who was still deeply and freshly affected by the grief of losing all that he loved, tried to alter his mortal past, only to be totally crushingly and completely and effortlessly defeated by the shadow of the afterthought of his future self (not even the actual physical future Godric... the future Godric is so powerful that his mere infinitesimal shadow of his afterthought can completely stomp all the combined Godric of his past selves with 0 effort. NOTE: just imply this in the story, don't show a scene where you have actual all godrics from all timelines fighting together against future Godric--it makes no sense.). VERY IMPORTANT FOR YOU: future Godric did not cause or manipulate or orchestrate the fall of Olympus, did not cause deaths of his beloved family or Thorin, thus you must not say that he made those deaths to cause the stasis event (Godric is not a monster, he will never willingly kill his beloved wife, children, and his best friend). Those tragedies were genuine. However, future Godric, not Thorin’s incomplete spell (who everyone else thought to be the cause of the stasis event), is the one who created the Stasis Event--Thorin's spell was a normal teleportation spell (to no one surprise really, there is no way a mortal can create a spell that is as potent as the one which initiates the stasis event and birthed the strongest apex predator god like Godric–there is only one being in existence who can do it: future Godric).

Since the instant Godric gained omniscience, he had always known the true origin of the stasis event. He knew he could not change it, but driven by grief he decided to try to save Olympus anyway, only to brutally discover his one and only weakness: he cannot overpower his future self's will.

Write a detailed realization that the current Godric is already so insanely powerful (he's actually the most powerful in the entire omniverse by infinite margin) that there is no way to imagine the scale of future Godric's, and how unfair and scary that what Godric considered to be his only weakness is his own future version, which makes it not really a weakness–it actually can be considered as additional strength to Godric’s already insane powers, since it means his future is guaranteed (and in that future, he’s even more omnipotent and powerful), and it also means that none of Godric’s power mechanics (amplification, superpower genesis, absolute concealment, absolute omniscience, weakness paradox, immune system, etc. can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else, since the origin of that power is someone who’s the most powerful being ever. You might suggest some ideas about the motive of future Godric creating the Stasis Event, but you must keep it clear that it is just a speculation (and please... don't suggest that it's because future Godric is threatened; he's ridiculously overpowered by then--nothing can even remotely threaten him... don't suggest any stupid moral lesson for future Godric...). You need to portray the current Godric as a king who is no longer troubled by his "weakness" or inability to alter his past anymore--he has accepted and even become amused and comfortable with it too. Kaedan must feel extreme existential dread at the end.
