content:
In the Year 1,000,047, when Kaedan was sixty-nine years old and the edges of his black court robes had begun to carry the faint silver weight of long service, Godric came to him without summons and without attendants. They walked together through the lower corridors of the palace, past the humming vaults where the journals slept, past the sealed doors behind which old instruments of suffering still dreamed. The air grew colder and older the farther they descended, until Kaedan smelled wet stone and the mineral hush of a place that had been closed for a very long time. He realized then that they were going to the sanctuary. The first room. The hidden wound where Godric had slept for ten thousand years while his body became something no language could hold.

The door was not locked. It opened at a touch, and Godric stepped inside as naturally as a man entering his childhood home. The chamber was not large. The walls were raw, ancient stone, streaked with mineral veins that had never seen sunlight. At the center stood a low altar, smooth and dark, and Kaedan’s stomach turned because he knew that his own bloodline had stumbled into this place a million years ago and changed all things by opening the wrong seal at the right time. Godric did not speak at first. He moved to the altar and rested his broad palm on its surface. He wore a plain dark tunic, and his salt-and-pepper hair caught the faint green light of the old stones. He looked, as always, exactly forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, heavy with muscle and impossible calm.

“You have served me for forty-seven years,” Godric said. His voice filled the small chamber without echo. “You have read the journals. You have learned to breathe around the size of me. You are no longer the boy who asked whether I was lonely. You are a man now, and I think it is time you understood the one thing none of the journals can say.”

Kaedan stood near the doorway, his hands folded into his sleeves to hide their tremor. “There is nothing the journals cannot say, Uncle. They have said enough to keep me awake for half a century.”

Godric turned. His face was warm, the same beloved face that had smiled at Kaedan’s childhood fevers and attended his father’s deathbed. But his eyes were on some other distance, and Kaedan had learned that expression. It was the look the King wore when he was about to unwrap an old truth and set it down in the middle of the room like a burning child.

“I have one true weakness,” Godric said.

Kaedan’s breath went out of him as if he had been struck under the ribs. The words did not belong in the same room as the man who had erased the omniverse with an accidental greeting from an unborn aura. They did not belong in the same universe as the being whose resting heartbeat had flattened creation and restored it before the dust could settle.

“That cannot be,” Kaedan said. “I have seen the records. I have watched the stars die and return because you let a new passive field say hello. What weakness could you possibly have?”

“I cannot undo the timeline before the Stasis Event,” Godric said. “Not in any way that would change my mortal past. I cannot travel to that time and stop Thronegate’s attack. I cannot reach the wedding day and carry Reina from the fire. I cannot stand before Isabel and Hebe and change the angle of a falling lintel. I can move through any other timeline. I can overpower causality anywhere else. But the period before the Stasis Event is sealed. It is the one place in all existence where my will does not move. It is the only avenue closed to me.”

Kaedan’s mouth opened, but no words came. In his chest, a cold wind stirred through the leaves of old assumptions. He had grown up believing that Godric was absolute, that every boundary had been burned away in the stasis, that the King could rewrite creation with an idle thought. And all of that was true. But now there was a wall, and the wall had a shape. The sanctuary felt smaller. The stone pressed against his back.

“I knew it from the beginning,” Godric continued. “From the first instant of my omniscience, when I opened my eyes on this altar, I knew the true origin of what had happened to me. I did not discover it years later. I woke with the knowledge already burning in me, already complete. I knew exactly why I could not save them. And still, because I was freshly carved open, because grief had not yet learned to live beside eternity, I tried.”

He walked a slow half circle around the altar, the heels of his boots making no sound on the stone.

“I tried, Kaedan. I tried to travel backward past the threshold. I had been King of Thronegate for a handful of months. He thought I was still half-mad with loss, and you would be right. I reached for the past with the full shape of my power, all of it, every amplified layer, every superpower, every passive shield, every sentient aura. I did not need to gather them. They were already there. I simply leaned into the direction of Before. And the seal stopped me.”

Godric paused. Kaedan could hear the faint, distant dripping of water somewhere in the darkness beyond the chamber.

“What stopped you?” Kaedan whispered. “If you had all of that, what could possibly stop you?”

“The shadow of an afterthought,” Godric said. “That is the exact description. Not my future self. Not his full body. Not even a single intention aimed at me. The seal was held in place by the shadow of an afterthought left behind by the man I will become. It was an echo so small that if it had been divided into every fraction of every second since time began, the largest remaining piece would still have been too small to name. And yet, when I pushed against it, I was crushed. Effortlessly. Completely. Not harmed. Not injured. Simply refused. The wall did not attack me. It declined me. It was the most absolute defeat I have ever experienced, and it was not a fight. It was a correction.”

Kaedan felt his skin go cold. He had seen Godric described as the apex predator, the ending of all endings. He had accepted that truth so deeply it had become part of his own heartbeat. But now he was being asked to hold another shape in his mind. The shape of something that could make the apex predator feel like a child pressing a palm against a continent.

“If every version of me from every previous instant had joined that attempt,” Godric said, “if every Godric that had existed from the moment the Stasis Event began until the moment of my reaching had added his full power to mine, it would not have changed the outcome. I did not need to test that. I felt it. The refusal was so complete that it made the entire history of my ascension feel like a long, soft whisper being asked to move a mountain.”

He came to a stop beside Kaedan, close enough that the warmth of his body reached through the cold air. The warmth felt monstrous now. It was the same warmth that had held Kaedan as a child, but it was also the warmth of a being who had been denied by his own future and had walked away from that denial without a scar.

“But you stopped trying,” Kaedan said. “You have not spent eternity fighting it.”

“No,” Godric said. “At first, I was crushed. I will not pretend otherwise. There was a stretch of hours, perhaps days, after that failure when I sat in the throne room and did not move. I did not need to move. I did not need anything. All the power in existence was still growing inside me, and I could not spend one sliver of it on the only thing that had ever mattered. Reina was still ash. Isabel was still burning. Hebe was still under the stone. And the future version of me, the ultimate one, had closed the only door that led back to them. That was a very black hour, Kaedan. I did not like it.”

He smiled then, and the smile was not bitter. It was the smile of a man remembering a cold morning he had long since left.

“But I accepted it,” he said. “I am comfortable with it now. Amused, even. Because when you look at the truth from the right angle, it is not a weakness. It is a guarantee. My only limitation is the power of my own future self. That means the future is already written, and in that future I am so much greater that the current me is reduced to nothing by comparison. It means no one can ever unmake what I am, because what I am was authored by the one being in existence who cannot be overpowered by anyone or anything. It means the very mechanics of my ascension, the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox, the immune system, all of it, are irrevocably sealed. No external force can exploit them. No enemy can tamper with their source. The source is Godric. The source is me, later, beyond all threat. How can I call that a weakness? It is another layer of armor.”

Kaedan tried to swallow. His throat had dried into a narrow passage. He understood the logic, but understanding it only made the fear darker. The only entity that could defeat Godric was Godric again, immeasurably older and infinitely stronger. That meant every possible future contained another Godric, larger and more terrible than the one before him. There was no end. There was no outside. There was no version of the omniverse where the apex predator was not already waiting ahead of the road.

“The Stasis Event came from him,” Kaedan said slowly. “Not from Thorin’s spell.”

“Yes,” Godric said. “Thorin did not create the Stasis Event. He only cast a forbidden teleportation spell from his bloodline, the same kind the old wizards used to cross deep distances when time was short. It was real. It saved me. It carried me from the burning wedding pavilion to this sanctuary. But it could not have done more. A mortal spell cannot generate the engine that turned me into this. No mortal could have crafted such a thing. Only one being in all existence could have reached back to that moment and rewritten the foundation of my flesh. My future self did it. He anchored his will into Thorin’s spell at the instant of my arrival, and the Stasis Event began. The deaths were not his doing. He did not kill Reina. He did not crush Hebe. He did not put the fire on Isabel. Thronegate did that. Ordinary mortal cruelty did that. The tragedy was real. But the transformation afterward was his.”

“Why?” Kaedan asked. “Why would he do it?”

Godric tilted his head. For a moment, he looked genuinely curious, as if the question were a small insect he had never bothered to examine. “I have speculations. But only speculations. Perhaps he needed to ensure that the loop of his own becoming would stay intact. Perhaps, from his impossible height, he looked back at the man who had lost everything and chose to give him the only structure that could never fall. Perhaps the shape of my existence is not a line but a knot, and the knot had to be tied by the only hand strong enough to hold it. I do not know, Kaedan. And I will not pretend to know. The man who did this is so far beyond me that even my omniscience sees only the fact of his action, not the full architecture of his reasons. What I can tell you is this: he did not act from fear. There has never been anything in any era that could threaten him. He did not strike because he was worried. He did not seal the past because some rival was approaching. Nothing can approach him. He is the final version of me, and that version does not respond to necessity. He acts because he can. That is the only honest answer.”

The cold in the chamber had grown heavy. Kaedan pulled his robes tighter, but the chill came from inside his own blood. He looked at the altar and imagined a young merchant’s hand touching the old seal, waking a dormant god from ten thousand years of silent amplification. He had always believed the Stasis Event was a cosmic accident, the wild result of a dying wizard’s last spell. The truth was worse. The truth was order. The truth was a future so powerful that it had already shaped the past before the past could shape itself.

“Then your only weakness is not a weakness at all,” Kaedan said. “It is the proof that no one can ever defeat you. Even if someone were mad enough to try, they would not be fighting only you. They would be fighting the fact of your future self. They would be fighting the origin of your powers, and that origin is beyond everything.”

“Correct,” Godric said. “It cannot be exploited. It cannot be used against me. The moment an enemy begins to imagine that the sealed past is a path they can walk, the Weakness Paradox engages, and they have already fed me another permanent amplification. But the paradox does not undo the seal, because the seal was placed by the one being whose will the paradox itself belongs to. The seal and the paradox are not opposed. They are both me, older and younger, pressing in the same direction. The enemy is not between them. The enemy is beneath them.”

He smiled again, and the smile was warm. That was the part Kaedan could never reconcile. The warmth was real. The man who spoke had loved him since birth, had sat at his father’s sickbed, had sent honey bread to his rooms when he was young. And the man was saying that no boundary existed anymore, because every possible route to his defeat was already closed by a version of himself too vast to see.

“Do you want to know what happened to the last creature that tried to use this weakness?” Godric asked. His voice had softened, but the softness was not mercy.

Kaedan did not want to know. He knew Godric would tell him anyway.

“It was a scholar-king from a line of temporal surgeons,” Godric said. “Very learned. Very patient. It had spent two hundred thousand years piecing together the shape of my past. It finally understood, in a shadowed approximation, that I could not cross the pre-Stasis threshold. It believed this meant the path to my origin was open to lesser hands. It built a needle designed to pierce the moment before the Stasis Event and unravel my mortal form before the future could anchor itself. The plan was, from a mortal perspective, elegant. It was also meaningless. The scholar-king never reached the threshold. The seal met it first. The shadow of my future self’s afterthought did not even need to rise. It simply let the scholar-king perceive the edge of the wall for one instant. The scholar-king’s mind was not destroyed. It was folded backward into that single instant and stitched there, so that it must live the same realization over and over, forever, with no pause and no death. I could have ended it. I did not. I stood at a window and listened. The sound it made was very regular, like a wet bell rung from the bottom of a well. I found it soothing.”

He looked at Kaedan with no shame, no discomfort. “I am not a kind being to those who oppose me, Kaedan. You know this. The court wizards have always known this. That scholar-king’s descendants were not restored when the rest of creation was later mended. I left them as they were, with the memory of their ancestor’s scream ringing through their bloodline. They do not approach Thronegate now. They do not approach anything. They wait for the sound to stop, and it never will.”

Kaedan’s fingers had gone numb inside his sleeves. He had known the King was cruel. He had read about the screaming chair arm and the pebble in the boot. But hearing Godric speak of it in his warm, conversational voice, in the same chamber where he had once slept, made the cruelty absolute. There was no hidden guard in Godric’s heart that rose up to punish his own evil. There was no moment of moral pause. There was only the calm, satisfied architecture of a predator who had long since stopped seeing any difference between justice and appetite.

“And you are no longer troubled by the fact that you cannot save them,” Kaedan said. “Olympus. Your wife. Your daughters. Thorin.”

Godric’s expression did not change. “I would not be human if I had never mourned them. I did mourn them. I still carry them, Kaedan. But I am no longer troubled by my inability to alter the past. That failure belongs to a much younger god, the one who had just become King and still thought he could reach through time to fix what time had already broken. I am not that god anymore. I am far beyond him. I am so far beyond him that he would not be able to perceive my shadow if I stood in front of him. And I am content. The future is guaranteed. The origin is sealed. The only thing I cannot do is the one thing that would have kept me small. In a certain light, that is not a wound. It is a mercy. It is the last mercy my own future self ever showed me.”

Kaedan thought he might be sick. The stone floor seemed to tilt, and he put a hand against the wall to steady himself. The revelation was too large. It had too many edges. Godric could not save the dead because his future self had sealed the past, and this was supposed to be the great weakness, but it was not a weakness at all. It was a cage that kept every possible enemy from ever touching his origin. It was a lock that could not be opened by anyone except a being that had never existed and never would exist. It was the ultimate unfairness. The one flaw in the apex predator was that he was guaranteed to become even stronger, and that guarantee was enforced by the strongest version of himself to ever exist.

“Then you were never in danger,” Kaedan whispered. “Not now. Not then. Not even before the Stasis Event. Because the event was already made. The future was already there. The whole shape of your life was already held in a closed hand.”

Godric nodded once, slowly, as if acknowledging a child’s first correct answer. “That is the truth of omniscience meeting the truth of origin. I always was. I always will be. And the greater I has already extended backward to make the lesser I. There was never a moment when I was only mortal. There was a moment when I believed I was mortal, but the seal was already placed. The loop was already closed. I only had to wake up.”

He stepped away from the altar and put a hand on Kaedan’s shoulder. The weight of it was terrifyingly light. “That is why I brought you here. Not to hurt you. Not to frighten you. But because you are my family, and family should know what house they live in. You have spent your life serving a king whose only weakness is that his future self is even more powerful than he is. Do you understand what that means for everyone else?”

Kaedan looked into Godric’s eyes. The question was not rhetorical. Godric wanted him to say it.

“It means there is no hope,” Kaedan said. “No hope at any point in time. No version of existence where a rebellion succeeds. No era where an enemy can win. Not because they are weak, though they are. Not because they lack weapons, though all their weapons are nothing. But because even if someone could discover a weakness, the weakness is not a doorway. It is a wall. And the wall is you.”

Godric’s smile widened, warm and terrible. “Exactly. And because the wall is me, no one can stand on the other side of it and call themselves safe. The future is mine. The past is mine. The present is the only room where lesser things can pace, and they can only pace because I leave the door open. Opposing me has never been a gamble. It is not even an error. It is a shape that reality briefly allows before I close my hand.”

He lifted his hand from Kaedan’s shoulder and began to walk back toward the door. The green light from the old stone walls traced the lines of his enormous back as he moved, and Kaedan saw again the heavy architecture of his body, the carved breadth of his shoulders, the silent weight of a man who had not needed to train for a million years. The muscles moved under the tunic like continents shifting in a world that belonged entirely to him. Kaedan thought of the journals, the stat tests, the superpower tests, the immune system, the auras. All of it had been zero percent. All of it had been the mildest possible breath from a being who was already beyond infinity. And now he knew that behind even that being stood another one, older and greater, whose shadow of an afterthought could crush him. The hierarchy of power had no top. It only had Godric, rising forever above himself.

“I should hate this,” Kaedan heard himself say. “The unfairness. The impossibility. But I cannot. I love you. I have always loved you. And I know now that love will not protect me from what you are. It only makes the fear more intimate.”

Godric paused at the door. He did not turn around. “I know, Kaedan. I have always known. That is why you are still standing here, and why the scholar-king is still ringing at the bottom of the well. Love is not a shield against me. But it is a reason I allow you to remain close. Do not mistake closeness for safety. You are close enough to see the fire. You are close enough to feel its shape. That is the highest mercy I can give anyone, and it is not a gentle mercy. It is only the amount of heat I choose not to release.”

He stepped through the door, and Kaedan followed, because there was nothing else to do. The corridor swallowed them both, and behind them the sanctuary returned to its deep silence. Kaedan’s bones had begun to ache with a cold that did not come from the stone. He thought of Reina, Isabel, Hebe, and Thorin, dead in the smashed garden ten thousand years before the world had learned to worship his uncle. He thought of the Stasis Event rising out of their disaster like a second sunrise, authored by a future too large to see. He thought of Godric standing at a window, listening to a scholar-king scream in an endless loop, and finding the sound soothing. The horror was not that Godric had a weakness. The horror was that the weakness made him untouchable, and he knew it, and he found it comfortable.

At the top of the stairs, the warm palace light returned, and Kaedan saw the shape of his own old hands clinging to his robes. The journals would one day need a new entry. He would write it, if he survived the night. He already knew the ending. It was the same ending every journal reached. Godric does not merely win. Victory against him was impossible before opposition began, and now the origin of impossibility had a name. It was the same name as the king. It was only later, larger, and still rising.

The year was written as a string of nines that had long ago stopped meaning anything to the men and women who kept the calendars. It was too large to write, too large to carve into stone, too large to hold in a single mind. The palace that stood at the center of all things was not built of marble or gold or even of compressed stars, because those materials had become too temporary for the King’s tastes. The palace was built from the structural memory of realities that had already ended, laid one over another in a single impossible architecture that held itself up through a million contradictory geometries. The floors were smooth as quiet water and dark as a closed eye. The walls shifted when no one was looking, adjusting their proportions so that every hall felt both infinite and private. The light came from no sun. It came from the slow combustion of dead timelines, soft and amber, like the last warmth of a body that would never finish cooling.

Clive was fifty years old. He was the Court Wizard of Thronegate, the direct descendant of Blake, the last son of the long line that had served the King since the old days when the King still had a face that mortals could describe. Clive’s black robes were heavy with inherited sigils, and his blood carried the same thousandfold daily amplification that had been placed in his ancestor’s veins a universe of years ago. That gift had been considered overwhelming once. It had driven previous court wizards to write trembling journals and hide their shaking hands in their sleeves. Clive did not write journals. The older journals were locked in a cold room beneath the palace, and no one opened them anymore, because the fear they described had become too small. They spoke of gods who could shatter galaxies and erase the omniverse, but the King had since grown beyond the range of those words.

The day began with the Song of the Green Hall. Clive stood near the central staircase and watched the palace’s master gardener move through the hedgerows that bordered the western colonnade. The gardener was not a man. The gardener had once been a living constellation, a being whose body had been a lattice of shining stars bound by their own collective identity. She had been called the Weeping Radiant, sovereign of ninety thousand burning systems, and in the old era she had been worshipped by a trillion species. Now she knelt in the soil, her hands wrapped in thick cloth, pulling a stubborn root free from a bed of pale blue flowers. Her glow had been dimmed to a faint silver shimmer, just bright enough to see. Her robes were patched and ordinary. She spoke to the flowers while she worked, her voice low and musical, and the flowers leaned toward her as though they remembered being something more.

Clive stopped beside her. “The King liked the blue ones best,” she said without looking up. “They only bloom when someone tells them the truth. I have been lying to them since morning.”

“Does it help?” Clive asked.

“No,” the gardener said. “But it passes the time.”

Another servant passed them, carrying a pile of folded cloth. He was a hulking shape, broad as a doorway, with too many joints and a face that did not fit his skull correctly. He had been a war god once, Clive knew. A thing of iron hymns and endless campaigns, adored by every warrior species in the old omniverse. Now he folded linen in a quiet room and slept on a cot near the laundry. His eyes always moved toward the windows, as if he expected the horizon to fall on him. The other servants called him Quiet Tarr, and no one asked about the terrible hollow in his voice. It had been carved there by the last time he had looked directly at the King’s face without permission.

The palace was full of such creatures. An empress of time now swept the eastern stairs. A lord of silence now polished the brass rails. A woman who had once been the combined will of a billion psionic minds now arranged flowers in the morning rooms. They did not speak of how they had come to serve. Their fear was too old and too complete to share. But Clive had learned some of the stories. He knew that the Weeping Radiant had once watched the King walk through a field of dying stars and had been so overwhelmed by the sight of his passive warmth that her own constellations had begun to orbit him against her will. She had not opposed him. That was the important part. She had simply seen him, and the seeing had ended her dominion. Now she gardened, because the King liked gardens, and because even an ancient constellation needed somewhere to hide from the shape of her own awe.

Clive climbed the stair at the far end of the hall. The palace was quiet. The whole of creation had been quiet for a googolplexian span of years, because opposition had stopped completely. There were no rebellions. No conspiracies. No hidden empires sharpening blades in the dark. There were no whispers of defiance, not even the faintest pulse of resistance in the deepest mine of the most forgotten world. The omniverse had learned. Not through force. Not through alteration of the will. The King had never once reshaped a mind to remove the concept of rebellion. He believed in mortal resilience. He believed that lesser creatures should be allowed to choose their own smallness. And so the choice had remained free, and every free mind had eventually made the same decision. They stopped opposing him because opposition had become a joke whose punchline arrived before the opening line. They stopped because they understood that challenging him was not an act of bravery. It was an act of tedious suicide.

Clive reached the upper gallery and paused to look out over the central gardens. The King was there, far below, walking with his hands clasped behind his back. The sight of him was not painful, because his absolute concealment had evolved countless times and could now make his presence feel like anything he wished. Today it felt like a warm breeze. Yesterday it had felt like the smell of old cedar. The day before, it had felt like the first hour after a fever breaks. The King could shape the atmosphere of his own existence without thought, and he did so absently, filling the palace with whatever texture pleased him. It was this control that allowed Clive to stand in his proximity without being erased. It was the only reason any of them could breathe.

Godric looked exactly as he always had. Forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, his frame heavy with muscle and his short salt-and-pepper beard neat against his jaw. He wore simple dark trousers and a loose white shirt. His arms were bare from the elbow down, and even at rest they showed the deep, sculpted mass of a man who had spent his mortal life lifting stone and wood and sword. The muscles no longer needed maintenance. They had long since become something beyond flesh, but they still held the memory of the king who had once been a mortal father walking through a garden before a wedding. He moved like a man enjoying the morning, his pace easy, his head tilted slightly to catch the sound of birds. The birds sang because he allowed them to sing. If he had wanted silence, the songs would have stopped before the birds understood the command.

Clive descended to the garden and approached. The air around Godric was warm and patient. The King turned as he approached, and his smile was the same smile Clive had known since childhood. It was a smile that reached his eyes and made him look like the kindest man in any universe. It was not a mask. It was the truth of him. The warm, friendly father still existed at the core of the tyrant, and the two were not at war. They were simply one being, made of both faces at once.

“Clive,” Godric said. His voice was low and rich, and it settled into Clive’s chest like a second heartbeat. “You are up early. I was just thinking about the old orchards. Do you remember the ones on Thronegate before the star changed color?”

“I remember the smell,” Clive said. “Apples and dust. The long road under the trees.”

Godric’s smile widened. “Yes. I liked that road. I walked it often when Blake was still alive. He used to complain that the dust ruined his boots. Then he would steal apples from the low branches and blame your ancestors for the missing fruit.” He chuckled, and the sound was soft and entirely human. “I miss him. The old days were simpler. But you know, I do not miss the weakness that came with them. Only the faces.”

They walked together along the hedge path. The gardener was still kneeling in the blue flowers, and she lowered her head as they passed. Godric did not look at her, but he raised one hand in a small greeting, and the air around her seemed to warm by a fraction of a degree. She made a quiet, almost inaudible sound, and Clive could not tell if it was gratitude or terror.

“The palace is calm today,” Godric said. “No one has so much as sighed in my presence for three millennia. It is peaceful. I used to enjoy the little rebellions, you know. When I first woke from the stasis, there were always some creatures who thought they could find a flaw. I let them come. I tested my strength on them, my speed, my magic. They were not threats. They were distractions. Brief little exercises to see how little of myself I needed to use. They always made me stronger, of course. The Weakness Paradox saw to that. But they were never exciting. They were like children throwing pebbles at the ocean. After a while, the children stopped throwing. The last true opposition occurred so long ago that I cannot recall its name without reaching backward through a number of years that would fill a library. It sent a fleet made from the stolen futures of eighty billion civilizations. I did not notice its approach until it was already inside the outer membrane of the palace grounds. Clive, when I say I did not notice, I mean that my passive systems had been waiting for it for so long that they had grown bored and fallen into a low state of idle watchfulness. The fleet was annihilated by one of my older auras before the first projectile finished leaving its barrel. The aura was the weakest of the sleeping set. It had been nerfed so long ago that even my own omniscience had to reach far back to find the command. The opposition did not die slowly. It simply stopped. There was no fire. No debris. Just a quiet lack of fleet. I felt the faintest touch of the aura’s satisfaction, like a cat catching a mouse in its sleep. That was the last day anything tried to oppose me. No one has tried since. They all learned, Clive. They all learned the absolute futility of it.”

He paused at a small stone bench and sat, inviting Clive to sit beside him. The bench was old, carved with the same ornamental vines that had been popular in Olympus before the fall. Godric ran his thumb along the armrest, and for a moment his gaze went far away.

“I did not force them to learn,” he said. “I have never altered the free will of a single creature. That would be dishonest. What would be the point of ruling over a garden of puppets? No, I left their will intact. I let them choose. And they chose silence. They chose obedience. They chose to serve my palace with their heads bowed and their hearts hammering. It is not a reflection of my mercy. It is a reflection of what happens when free will is given an honest look at the distance between us.”

Clive sat down carefully. The stone was cool, and the morning air smelled of the blue flowers and the damp earth of the gardener’s beds. He watched a small procession of servants cross the far colonnade, carrying trays of polished fruit. One of them was a former sun-god from a dead pantheon. His face was blank now, his movements precise and slow. He had seen the King’s face once from too near a window, and the memory had burned every other thought from him.

“They fear you,” Clive said. It was not an accusation. It was only the truth.

“Yes,” Godric said. “And I am friendly to them. I am friendly to all of them. I know their names. I know the names of their dead. I know the exact shape of the fear inside them, and I do not punish them for it. Fear is a reasonable response. I am not offended by it. I would be offended only by action. The gardener is terrified, but she tends my flowers. The old war god is terrified, but he folds my linen. They are useful, and they are loyal, and I am warm to them. That is the arrangement. It has held for a very long time.”

He leaned back and looked at the sky, where the slow combustion of dead timelines turned the clouds a soft gold. “Do you know what I am going to do today, Clive?”

“No, my King.”

Godric smiled, and the smile was almost mischievous, the expression of a man preparing to deliver a private and enormous joke. “I am going to reach backward. Far backward. Past all the years that have passed since my awakening. Past the first days of Thronegate’s rise. Past the stasis itself. I am going to touch the moment when I was still mortal, when my wife and daughters were still alive, when Olympus was still standing. And then I am going to ensure that I become what I am. Ensure.”

Clive’s blood went cold. He had heard of this moment from the older journals, the ones locked in the cold room, but he had never expected to witness it. “The Stasis Event,” he whispered. “You are going to create it.”

“I already did,” Godric said. “From your perspective, it has already happened. But from my perspective, the moment is now. I am the one who made it. I have always been the one who made it. The loop closes here, in this garden, on this morning, with me sitting on a stone bench beside the last of Blake’s line. The past is about to become my handiwork. I am not worried. I am not heavy. I am only amused by the scale of it.”

The words settled into Clive like a cold stone. He had always thought of the Stasis Event as an ancient catastrophe, an accident of dying magic that had transformed a grieving king into a god. But the King spoke of it as a craftsman speaks of a favorite chair. He had built it. He would build it. And the build had been finished before the first atom of the old world had ever existed.

“You could have made it more potent,” Clive said. “Couldn’t you? You could have granted your past self a stasis that matched everything you are now.”

Godric nodded, his eyes warm with approval. “I could have granted him a perfect copy of my current mechanisms. I could have reached into that old sanctuary and filled his sleeping body with the sentient auras as they are now, the passive shields as they are now, the evolved immune system, the amplification engine, the full recursion of the Weakness Paradox. I could have done it without cost. A single thought. Not even a thought. A momentary permission. He would have woken at Year Zero with power so far beyond the old version that the omniverse would not have been able to perceive him at all. But I chose to hold back.”

Clive frowned. The idea of Godric holding back was familiar, but never in this form. “Why?”

“Because I wanted him to have some mortal struggle,” Godric said. “I wanted him to remember what it felt like to be a man who had lost everything and still had to build himself back from the ruins. If I had given him all of this, he would have become a smooth and perfect engine from the first second. He would have crushed Thronegate without even remembering that he had once been small enough to hurt. I thought the held-back version would preserve a sense of struggle. I thought it would keep the old fire alive. I believed, in my sentimentality, that a smaller beginning would make the later growth feel more real. It was a ridiculous thought, of course. Even the version I held back was so incomprehensibly powerful that he woke from stasis already effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. His first act was not a struggle. It was a formality. There was never any mortal struggle. The scale was already broken. But I held back anyway, because I wanted him to have the story of a man who had to try. It was a gift. A small and incorrect gift.”

Clive’s mind was already moving into impossible territory. If Godric had held back, and the held-back version had made the Godric of Year Zero effectively infinite compared to creation, then the gap between the held-back version and the full version was wider than the gap between a single flicker and all the light that had ever existed. And that was only the beginning. Because the current Godric, the one sitting beside him, had grown from that held-back seed. His amplification had continued forever. His superpowers had multiplied forever. His auras, shields, immune system, and weakness paradox had evolved forever. He was the product of an infinite process layered on top of a beginning that had already made the rest of creation irrelevant. If he had instead chosen to grant his past self the full version, the starting point would have been greater, and therefore the process would have produced an even greater current Godric. And a greater current Godric could have granted an even greater past, which would have produced an even greater present, which could have granted an even greater past, and the loop would have multiplied endlessly, each recitation lifting the whole structure higher without any ceiling.

The realization hit Clive in the center of his chest. His lungs filled with air that suddenly felt too heavy to breathe. Godric could have made himself infinitely stronger by granting a stronger start to his past self, and then he would have been strong enough to grant an even stronger start, and that would have made him stronger still, and the process would have escalated beyond any scale that even the old journals could describe. But he had not done that. He had chosen to hold back. He had chosen a single version, and even that single version had made all opposition impossible. The restraint was not mercy. It was a kind of infinite restraint, the refusal of an infinite ladder because the view from the first rung was already too high to bother climbing. The unfairness of it was so absolute that Clive had to close his eyes for a moment and grip the edge of the bench.

“You are beginning to see it,” Godric said softly. “The cause and effect. The loop that could have swallowed itself and grown fatter forever. I did not choose that loop. I did not need to. I am already beyond the point where such choices matter. My present self is so far above my past selves that the act of granting them more or less is only a kind of nostalgia. I gave my past the held-back version because I remembered what it felt like to be a man who wanted to struggle. But I did not need the struggle myself, and he did not need it either. The struggle was already over the moment the first Planck second of the stasis passed.”

He rose from the bench and turned toward the garden’s far edge. The gardener was still working, her silver glow faint against the blue flowers. The war god was folding linen in a nearby alcove. The sun-god was carrying fruit. All of them moved with the heavy, reverent terror of creatures who had been allowed to live inside the shadow of a force they could never measure. Not one of them looked at Godric directly. They had learned that looking was too much.

“Now I am going to do it,” Godric said. “I am going to reach back to Year Minus Ten Thousand. I am going to find Thorin mid-incantation, his lungs full of blood, his spell already breaking open the air. I am going to let the teleportation carry my past self to the sanctuary, just as it always did, and then I am going to touch that arrival with the stasis. I will not kill anyone. I will not alter Thronegate’s attack. I will not save Reina. I will not move Hebe out from under the stone. Those events are fixed, not because I made them, but because they happened. I am not the author of the fall. I am only the author of what came after. The deaths of my family were genuine. The fire was genuine. Thronegate’s betrayal was genuine. My future self can hold back all he likes, but he cannot change that. He will not change that. He will only close the loop, as always, by making the man who survived into something that could survive everything.”

He lifted his hand. It was a small motion, no larger than the movement a man might make to brush a leaf from a branch. But Clive felt the temperature of the whole garden change. The light from the dead timelines dimmed. The birds stopped singing. The gardener dropped her trowel and covered her face. Every servant in the palace froze in place, their eyes wide, their hands pressed to their chests. The air grew very still, and then it grew very old, and then it seemed to turn sideways, exposing the hidden seam between the present and the deep past.

Godric’s fingers closed once. The motion was gentle. It was the closing of a hand around an invisible thread. Clive saw, or thought he saw, a brief flash of something on the far side of the air, a high white room, a falling column, a man with salt-and-pepper hair screaming as the world came apart. He saw a wizard falling with a spear through his skull. He saw a dark sanctuary, wet stone, the first glimmer of stasis wrapping around a body that would sleep for ten thousand years. Then the flash was gone, and the garden library again, and the birds were singing, and Godric was lowering his hand with the calmness of a man who had just finished turning a page.

“It is done,” Godric said. “You have just witnessed the origin of me. The loop is closed. My past self is asleep in the sanctuary, already amplifying for the first time, already receiving the first of his superpowers, already wrapped in the absolute concealment that will keep the omniverse from shattering around him. He will wake. He will become King. He will build Thronegate into an empire. He will meet Blake, and his line will continue, and one day, after the googolplexian years, a court wizard named Clive will stand in a garden and watch his King close the loop. It is elegant, isn’t it? A closed circle with no outside and no inside. Only the shape of me, repeated.”

Clive’s knees were weak. He wanted to sit again, but his body would not move. The magnitude of what he had just seen was too large. It was not the act itself that frightened him. It was the ease of it. The King had reached across the whole of time, touched the oldest wound in his own history, and stitched it into place with a single small closing of his fingers. He had not raised his voice. He had not gathered power. He had not even seemed to notice the full weight of what he had done.

“You are quiet,” Godric observed. “That is appropriate. Words would not hold this moment. But I want you to understand one more thing. Do not look away.”

He turned to face Clive, and the warmth in his expression was still there, but it was deeper now, older, as though the man’s face were being illuminated from inside by a light that had been burning since the first universe. “The version of the Stasis Event I just created is the held-back version. The one I chose long ago, with all its limits intact. It is not the full version. It is not the version I could have made. And I know, because I have just done it, that I could have made the stronger version at no cost. I could have given him the evolved auras, the evolved shields, the evolved immune system, the full recursion of the evolved Weakness Paradox. I did not. I held back. And here is the piece you must carry in your mind, Clive. The full version would not have made my past self stronger by a finite amount. It would have made him stronger by an amount that would have rewritten the early history of my entire ascension. That stronger beginning would have fed forward into every later iteration of me, and each later iteration would have been able to reach back and grant a stronger beginning still. The loop would have become an infinite spiral of increasing origin. I did not choose that spiral. I chose the smaller version. The weaker version. And the weaker version still produced a Godric who, at Year Zero, was already effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. Are you beginning to feel the shape of it?”

Clive nodded. He could not find his voice. The garden was peaceful around them, but the peace felt like a thin skin stretched over an abyss. He understood that he was standing beside a being whose past self’s weakest form had been beyond all conceivable challenge, and whose present self had grown beyond that by an infinite process repeated an unthinkable number of times, and whose future self, if such a term still meant anything, would make the present self look like a flicker dying on a wet stone.

“The old journals used to call me an apex predator,” Godric said. “They called me the ultimate tyrant. They spoke of my sentient auras as if they were terrifying. Gent used to be the weakest. The journals wrote about Gent with trembling hands. Do you know what Gent is now, Clive? Gent is a memory. The sentient auras have evolved so many times that Gent’s oldest version has been folded into the foundations of my passive architecture. It is still there, but it is no longer distinct. It is a single thread in a garment that now has more threads than there have ever been moments in all of time. The newer auras do not simply neutralize threats. They do not simply pre-arrive before the thought of danger. They do not just remove hostile intent from every coordinate. The new auras are the creators of the conditions in which threat cannot be conceived. They hold the omniverse in a state of passive impossibility. The palace, the gardens, the dead timelines burning overhead, all of it is held inside their attention. They are so redundant that even the most paranoid of the old texts could not have guessed their number. And they are not needed. They love me. They serve me. They would erase existence if I asked, and I do not ask, because there is no longer anything worth erasing. The idea of opposition is not dead because I killed it. It is dead because the new auras have made the concept of an enemy into an old joke, and the joke has been retold so many times that it no longer has a punchline.”

He began to walk again, and Clive followed because his body knew the motion even when his mind was reeling. They moved past the gardener, who remained on her knees, her silver light shivering. They passed the old war god, who pressed himself against the colonnade wall and made a sound like a harmonica being slowly squeezed. They passed the sun-god, who dropped his tray of fruit and immediately began to weep, the tears pouring from his blank face and pattering against the floor.

“Look at them,” Godric said, not unkindly. “They are terrified. But they are not harmed. They will never be harmed. I like them, Clive. I like that they still know how to be afraid. It reminds me that free will still exists, even when all its choices have become the same choice. That is why I keep them. Not to humiliate them. Not to punish them. I keep them because I enjoy the company of creatures who can still feel the full weight of the distance between us. Their fear is the only thing left in creation that can hold a mirror to my presence. It is a small mirror. A cracked mirror. But it is enough.”

He stopped at the edge of the garden and looked out over the palace grounds, where the light from the dead timelines was beginning to shift into the deeper gold of afternoon. The birds had returned, and their songs filled the air with a fragile sweetness.

“I am an evil tyrant,” Godric said. “By every moral measure your line has ever invented. I have no pity for my enemies. I have no interest in their suffering except when it pleases me to notice. But I am not gratuitous. I do not destroy when there is nothing to learn. I do not create pain when the pain would have no witness. The gardener is useful, so she lives. The war god is useful, so he lives. You are useful, and you are loved, so you live. That is the whole moral structure of my reign. Usefulness and love, in that order. The rest of creation exists because I have not yet found it inconvenient. Is that evil? Yes. It is evil. It is an evil so large that no single language can hold it. But it is also warm. It is also stable. It is also the only reason any of you are still breathing. I am not a monster, Clive. I am the king of monsters. The difference is that a monster kills, and I choose not to. That choice is the only mercy I have ever needed, and it is an endless mercy. The universe sleeps because I allow it to sleep. It will never wake.”

Clive looked at the King’s broad back, at the heavy swell of his shoulders under the white shirt, at the easy power in his stance. He thought of the old journals, the trembling wizards, the broken quills and the bile-stained ink. They had been afraid of the zero-percent world. They had been afraid of a Godric who could erase the omniverse with a blink. They had not known that the blink was the held-back version. They had not known that even the held-back version was itself held back from a greater held-back version, and that the greater held-back version could have been at the center of an infinite spiral of origin. They had not known that all their fear was only the shadow of a shadow, cast by a light that would never fully reach them.

“Do you want to know the truth that will keep you awake tonight?” Godric asked, not looking back. “The weakest of my sentient auras, reduced by an infinite recursion of nines, allowed to express only the smallest possible fraction of itself, could still catch the entire omniverse in a single passive yawn and unmake it before the yawn finished forming. And I have not used that aura in a googolplexian years. It has grown so far beyond its old self that the old self would not recognize it. The old self would call the new self impossible. And the new self is only one of countless trillions of passive systems layered around me. The truth is not that no one dares oppose me. The truth is that the universe itself has stopped daring. It waits. It breathes. It folds its linen and waters its flowers. And I walk through it, friendly and warm, because that is the only face that does not make the servants drop their trays.”

He turned then, and his smile was gentle, but his eyes were the oldest thing Clive had ever seen. They were not cruel. They were not hungry. They were filled with the easy, absolute contentment of a creature whose every need had already been met before the need could form.

“Come,” Godric said. “Let us go inside. The palace has grown too quiet, and I would like to hear the gardener sing before the evening comes.”

Clive followed him through the colonnade, past the weeping sun-god and the quivering war god, past the gardener still kneeling among the blue flowers, and into the endless, impossible palace where the floors were made from the memory of ended realities and the walls shifted when no one was watching. The King walked with his hands behind his back, his broad body filling the corridor with a warmth that felt like the first hour of spring, and Clive understood that he would spend the rest of his life carrying the knowledge that all of it, every stone, every servant, every flickering timeline, was held in the palm of a single being who had already chosen to hold back forever. The horror was not that Godric was evil. The horror was that he was patient, and warm, and in no hurry to let go.

Roth had spent nineteen years trying to learn the exact shape of Godric’s sense of humor. He had failed in every meaningful way, and the morning of the visit began with another failure. The King materialized in the court wizard’s private study not through the door, but from the space between one paragraph of a book and the next, as if he had always been standing there and the room had only now caught up. He held two traveling cloaks over one arm and something in his other hand that looked like a hat had been beaten to death and then forgiven. Godric was grinning, his salt-and-pepper beard neat against his jaw, his massively muscled frame already half-turned toward the wall as though he expected Roth to follow without question.

“We are going on a little trip,” Godric said. “The Last Confluence is holding its final muster. Tomorrow is the big day. I thought we should see the show before the show.”

Roth put down his pen. His own blood carried the thousandfold daily amplification that had been placed in his ancestor Blake’s line a million years ago, and by any standard outside the King’s shadow, Roth was a walking cataclysm. He could crack a planet with a suppressed flicker of arcane force. He could boil the mana out of a hostile god’s bones. But standing in the same room as Godric, he felt like a damp leaf pasted to the underside of a landslide. The King’s absolute concealment made the feeling bearable, but it could not make it small.

“The Last Confluence has been preparing for forty thousand years,” Roth said carefully. “They call themselves the largest free coalition in existence. They believe they are hidden.”

Godric’s grin widened. “I know. That is the fun part. They have been hidden from every power in the omniverse, which means nothing, because I have known their every whispered plan since before their first great-grandfather learned to sharpen a knife. They survived because I allowed it. They will attack tomorrow because I am curious how much of the attack I will notice. Now put this on.”

He tossed one of the cloaks at Roth. The cloth was ordinary, rough and brown, with a hood that smelled faintly of wagon dust. Then Godric produced the rest of his disguise. A floppy cap with a fat crimson feather. A pair of violet spectacles that did not sit straight. A false black mustache so wide it looked like a horse’s tail glued to his upper lip. He put the cap on first, then the spectacles, then pressed the mustache over his own real mustache and the upper part of his short salt-and-pepper beard. The false mustache pointed slightly left. His real beard still showed beneath it, perfectly trimmed and undeniable.

“You look,” Roth said, “exactly like the King of Thronegate wearing a false mustache.”

Godric adjusted the feather. “Nonsense. I am Rogo the Cheese Commissioner from the Free Satrapies. I am here to inspect the army’s rations. No one will suspect a thing.”

Roth looked at the ceiling. He loved this man. He had loved him since he was a child, when Godric had sat beside his sickbed and told him stories about old Thronegate markets. The love was real, and so was the cold waterfall of dread. Godric had erased the omniverse before with less than an accidental breath from an unborn aura. The journals in the lower vault were full of men like Roth, and every one of them had written the same sentence in different trembling hands: he does not know how large he is. The terrible thing was that Godric did know. He knew everything. He simply found the gap between his power and the world funny.

Godric opened a door in the far wall. The door had not existed a moment earlier. Beyond it, the smell of hot iron and charred incense rolled in, and Roth saw a red sky stretched over a fortress ring so enormous that its curve disappeared into the haze of a captured dead star. The King stepped through first, still holding his hat in place against a wind that did not exist. Roth followed because there was no other choice.

The Last Confluence had built its redoubt inside a folded gulf outside standard navigable space. It was a crescent of armored continents and fortress moons stitched together by tensile bridges of crystallized law, wrapped around a dying star whose light had been harnessed to power a trillion furnaces. The sky was not a sky. It was a dome of security fields through which Roth could see the outlines of docked warships beyond the veil, their hulls dripping with sensor chaff and phase-distortion wax. The air smelled of copper, old blood, and the bitter smoke of star-heart offerings. A low, unending hum rose from the foundries below, where entire species were forging their last weapons.

The two of them walked down a ramp made from the rib cage of something that had once been the size of a galaxy cluster. At the first checkpoint, a line of four-armed guards in black ceramic armor inspected cargo wagons and pass-slips. Each guard carried a sidearm that Roth’s amplified senses identified immediately as a personal causality shearer, a weapon designed to sever its target’s past from its present. It would have troubled a major god. Against Godric, it would do less than a moth against a burning mountain.

Roth handed over the travel passes he had prepared because Godric had told him to prepare them the night before. The lead guard squinted at the papers, then at Godric. His species had three eyes, and all three narrowed.

“Rogo the Cheese Commissioner,” the guard said slowly. “You are much larger than the last cheese commissioner.”

Godric spread his hands. His enormous shoulders filled the cloak, and the false mustache twitched. “I eat a great deal of the product.”

The guard looked at Roth. Roth produced a small iron medallion with the supply guild’s mark and flooded it with just enough charm magic to make the metal feel legitimate. It was not mind control. It was only bureaucratic misdirection. The guard grunted and waved them through. Roth felt a bead of cold sweat slide down his spine. He had not needed to fear the guard. He had needed to fear what would happen if the guard decided to raise his weapon. Godric was patient, but Godric was not safe.

The interior of the redoubt was a brutal city built for war. Streets were carved through black stone and lined with barricades stacked from the hull-plates of dead titans. Training yards the size of small moons held ranks of soldiers moving through synchronized drills. Roth saw species he had only read about in the old bestiaries. Star-scaled serpentine things rolling through the air. Insectoid battalions whose chitin was plated with stolen chronology. Living weapons grown from prayer and bone, seated in iron cradles, breathing in slow, wet gasps. The Confluence had gathered every splinter of the defeated, every remnant of every pantheon Thronegate had ever broken. They were not weak. By the standards of the old world, they were the greatest army ever assembled. But Roth’s own father had fought in the Thronegate expansion wars, and Roth knew the truth. This army was powerful the way a bucket is full. Godric was the ocean behind the ocean.

Godric strolled through the streets with his hands clasped behind his back. The feather in his cap bounced. The false mustache had begun to peel at the left edge, but he kept pressing it back with his thumb. He looked, Roth thought, like a friendly bear who had decided to enter a butcher’s shop and pretend to be a customer. Every few hundred paces, he paused to inspect something. A rack of null-lances. A row of chronal cavalry waiting in amber suspension. A great hopper full of shattered god-cores being melted down for armor polish. He made small sounds of appreciation, as if touring a vineyard.

A young officer with a shaved head and too many badges stepped into their path. He wore a yellow sash over his chest and carried a data-slate that hummed with nine different security frequencies. “You are the ration inspectors,” the officer said. “Good. Follow me. The High Council wants the eastern platforms verified before tonight’s address.”

Roth opened his mouth to make an excuse. Godric spoke first. “We would be honored. Lead the way, my boy.”

The officer led them along a moving causeway that carried them up through the lower tiers of the fortress. Roth watched Godric’s face as they passed the war shrines. The King was not gloating. He was genuinely interested. He looked at the black banners sewn with older sigils and the altar fires where priests had burned their own memories as offerings. He looked at the conscripted gods dragging heavy munitions carts, their shoulders bent under chains that had been blessed by their own old pantheons. There was no pity in his face. There was curiosity, and a kind of warm absence, the look of a man examining a child’s drawing.

“You have a great deal of material,” Godric said to the young officer. “How many will you commit tomorrow?”

The officer puffed out his chest. “All of them. Every free soul. The Confluence does not believe in reserve forces. If we fail, there will be no one left to fail.”

Godric nodded slowly. “That is a great many souls.”

“Better to die free than live in his shadow,” the officer said.

Godric looked at Roth, and Roth saw the corner of his mouth twitch under the false mustache. “You might get your wish.”

The causeway ended at a massive transit gate guarded by two statues that were not statues. They were dormant siege engines folded into the shape of hooded women. Their eyes tracked Roth and Godric as the officer presented his clearance. One of the hooded shapes leaned down, and its face opened into a vertical slit filled with rotating sensor crystals. It scanned Godric for six seconds. Roth felt the air change, and his own amplified defenses rose without his permission. Then the slit closed, and the siege engine returned to stillness.

“Cheese Commissioner,” it said, in a voice like metal being drawn through a sieve. “No contaminants detected. You may pass.”

Godric patted his own chest as if checking his pockets. “Wonderful. What a polite security system.”

The transit gate opened onto a wide observation platform above the central muster grounds. Below, Roth could see millions of soldiers arranged in blocks, their banners unfurled, their weapons held high. At the far end of the platform stood the High Council chamber, a vast domed hall made from fused causality glass. Inside, the war council was already gathered, and holographic displays hung in the air like burning mirrors. Godric and Roth entered through a side door reserved for functionaries, and no one looked up.

The Supreme Commander of the Last Confluence was a being called Volarion the Unbowed. He stood at the center of the table, towering over even the largest holograms. His body was shaped from interlocked plates of dark crystal and living muscle, and his face was a shifting arrangement of six vertical eyes. Across from him sat the High Oracle, Sephyss, a woman made of silver light and preserved memory. She did not speak. Her eyes were closed, and her lips moved in constant silent calculation. The Master of Arsenal, a creature named Kraec, stood near the far wall with his arms crossed over a mechanical chest that whined with every breath. He was not a natural life form. He had replaced most of his flesh with weapon systems centuries ago, and the remaining flesh had grown around the metal like moss.

The holograms showed the face of Godric from a dozen angles. Roth recognized the images. They were not accurate, but they were close enough. Some depicted him with a crown of black fire. Some showed his beard as a storm cloud. The council was planning an attack, and Roth could see the shape of it in the floating schematics. They meant to strike at dawn with seven synchronized null-lances, each aimed at a different iteration of the King across a different layer of time. The lances would be fired from a single weapon known as the Latter Oblivion, a black obelisk shielded beneath the central keep. The council was calling it the Deicide Chord. If it worked, they believed, every version of Godric would be unmade at once.

Godric watched the holograms with his head tilted. Roth stood close beside him, feeling the heat of the room and the pressure of his own heartbeat. The council was not speaking to them. They were too important for ration inspectors. But then Volarion turned his six eyes toward the side door and frowned.

“You,” the Supreme Commander said. “The cheese commissioner. Why are you here?”

Godric removed his cap and held it over his chest with an expression of wide innocence. “I was told to verify the rations. But I could not help hearing the plan. It is very ambitious.”

Volarion’s eyes flickered. “It is not ambitious. It is final.”

Godric put the cap back on. “Final is a very strong word. What if he does not come?”

“He will come,” Volarion said. “His arrogance demands it. He will stand before us and die.”

Godric turned to Roth and spoke in a voice that was clearly meant only for him, though the room was too small to hide it. “They are not wrong about the arrogance.”

The council returned to its planning. The High Oracle opened her eyes once. Roth saw her gaze pass across Godric’s face, and for a single instant her silver light flickered. Her lips stopped moving. Her hands rose from the table and gripped the edge as if the whole chamber had tilted. Then a counselor leaned close and asked a question about particle geometry, and Sephyss shook her head, closed her eyes, and resumed her silent calculations. Roth released the breath he had not known he was holding. The moment had passed, but not the terror inside it.

They left the chamber through a lower corridor and descended toward the foundry levels. The air thickened with heat and the smell of molten reality. Great engines pounded in the dark, and the walls sweated a black oil that glinted with pinprick stars. At the center of the deepest vault, surrounded by a wide walkway of polished stone, hung the Latter Oblivion. It was not a spear or a cannon. It was an obelisk of black material that seemed to consume the light around it, its surface carved with uncountable channels that leaked white fire. Time behaved strangely near it. Roth could feel the weight of its weaponry pressing against his own senses, and his amplified arcane perception immediately began to calculate the yield. The weapon was built to unmake every moment in which Godric had ever existed. The calculation shattered at once. Roth’s mind refused to finish it, because the answer at the end of the function was a number so large it would have erased the concept of measurement, and then the next thought came. The weapon was not large enough. It had never been large enough. Even the strongest weapon ever built by free hands was still only a weapon built by hands.

Godric walked up to the guardrail and leaned over. The technicians below were making final adjustments, and one of them called for a low-yield resonance check. A small lance discharged from a branch emitter, and the white line of energy crossed the vault. It was supposed to strike a null-stone effigy of Godric on the far side. The effigy vanished. But a stray arc from a cracked emitter split off and rose directly upward, crossing the guardrail and passing through Godric’s chest.

Roth felt his own heart seize. The arc vanished on contact, as if it had been swallowed by a surface that gave back nothing. Godric looked down at his coat, then brushed a speck of dust from the false mustache. “The air is dry here,” he said. “I felt a slight draft.”

A technician below waved up at them. “Calibration error. The safety suppressor caught it. No harm done.”

There was no safety suppressor. Roth had seen the arc vanish without passing through any field. Godric had simply been where the energy was, and the energy had ended. The King did not mention it. He turned from the rail and began to walk again, and Roth followed with his knees threatening to fold.

At the entrance to the eastern hall, a creature waited for them. It was not a soldier. It was a hound, but not the small, warm kind Roth had seen in the palace kennels. This hound was the size of a grain silo, with a long spine of exposed bone and a face made of overlapping sensory plates. It sat on its haunches and turned its broad head as they approached. The handler at its side tightened a chain of glowing silver.

“Don’t mind her,” the handler said. “She’s a reality hound. Trained to scent out Thronegate magic. She’ll take your hand off if you smell wrong.”

The hound lowered its head as Godric approached. Its sensory plates flushed a pale green. Then it rolled onto its back and presented its stomach, all four legs folding in the air. The handler stared.

“She never does that,” the handler said. “She hates everyone.”

Godric crouched, and Roth saw the massive muscles of his thighs shift under the merchant’s cloak. He scratched the hound behind the ear. “Good girl,” Godric said. “You have excellent instincts.”

The hound whined, and Roth did not know whether it was asking for more or begging to be released. The handler laughed uneasily and pulled the chain. Godric stood, and they continued toward the western gates.

That evening, the whole redoubt gathered for the final address. The muster grounds filled with billions of soldiers, and the air above them flickered with projector fields so that even those in the far tiers could see Volarion standing on the high balcony. Roth and Godric stood near the middle of the crowd, hemmed in by bodies that stank of oil, sweat, and the bitter perfume of last rites. A mother nearby lifted her child onto her shoulders. The child had four arms and a face like wet stone, and it pointed at Godric.

“Mother, who is that man with the silly mustache?” the child asked.

The mother looked. “A ration inspector, I think. Don’t stare.”

Godric waved at the child. The child waved back. Roth felt a sickness rising in his throat that had nothing to do with the smoke.

Volarion spread his arms, and his voice rolled out over the crowd, magnified by a thousand hidden speakers. “Tomorrow,” he said, “we erase the abomination from all existence. We have hidden our work for forty thousand years. We have burned our pasts to blind his eyes. We have sharpened our lances on the bones of our own dead. He does not know. He cannot know. Tomorrow, at dawn, we will strike the Thronegate tyrant from every moment at once, and the omniverse will breathe for the first time in a million years.”

The crowd roared. The roar was so loud that the frame of the redoubt shook, and loose dust rained from the black vault above. Roth saw Godric clapping. The false mustache had peeled halfway off his face, and he clapped with the rest of them, a warm and patient smile on his lips.

After the address, they walked toward the main gate. The path led through a narrow guardhouse where a veteran sentry stood watch. He was an old Thronegate desert world soldier, one of the few in the Confluence who had survived the early expansion wars. His face was a map of old burns, and his hands had been replaced with iron claws. When Godric passed through the gate, the sentry looked up. His jaw went slack. His claws opened and closed once, and then his eyes rolled back in his head. He fell against the wall without a word, sliding to the floor in a clatter of armor. The other guards rushed to him, calling for medics, and Godric stepped around them.

“He recognized me,” Godric said to Roth as they walked out into the red light of the captured star. “That one saw me at the burning of the Kaelen Front. I remember his face. He was a brave man. He tried to fire a siege lance at my left eye.”

Roth asked, “What will you do tomorrow?”

Godric shrugged. “I have not decided. I might let a new aura handle it. Or I might simply look at them. I have not used the full weight of my gaze in a very long time. It might be enjoyable to see how far the fear travels.”

They did not return to the palace through a door. Godric simply turned a corner at the edge of the redoubt, and the red light was gone, replaced by the warm golden hush of the royal solar. Roth stood on the familiar floor, his traveling cloak still smelling of smoke and copper, and he understood that the entire day had been a courtesy call. Not a reconnaissance. Not a threat. A courtesy call.

“I went because they spent forty thousand years planning,” Godric said, as if reading Roth’s thoughts. He was not reading them, Roth reminded himself. He simply already knew. “I wanted to see the shape of hope before it becomes another dirty spot on the floor. They were never close to anything, Roth. They were never even close to being wrong in a way that mattered. Tomorrow they will fire their Deicide Chord, and it will not reach me. It will not make me feel a tickle. It will barely be worth waking up for.”

He removed the floppy cap and set it on the arm of a golden chair. Then he peeled off the false mustache and tossed it aside. Underneath, his real face was calm, his salt-and-pepper beard neat, his eyes carrying the vast, ancient warmth that Roth had loved and feared since childhood. “But I will wake for it,” Godric said. “Because they worked so hard. And because you, my dear Roth, will write about it afterward, and I would not want to deprive you of the ending.”

He clapped Roth once on the shoulder, gently enough to nearly separate Roth’s soul from his body, and walked out of the solar humming an old Thronegate march. Roth stood alone in the warm light, listening to the sound fade, and he understood that the Last Confluence would not even have the dignity of an end. It would have a disappearance. It would have the exact quality of something that never existed, because when Godric finally allowed the smallest sliver of his attention to turn toward them, their forty thousand years, their billions of souls, their black obelisk and their Deicide Chord, all of it would be less than a single unfired word before a closed mouth.

Write a detailed story of Godric deciding to subjugate the IRL universe, at Year 25\.

Earth obviously, has 0 chance, and will experience total despair and existential dread.

In this scenario, you must make Earth try their best to kill Godric, which means Godric will completely annihilate it. You must NOT make Godric nice, forgiving. He can still be friendly. Godric feels mischievously playful so he doesn't instantly finish it (you must ensure the reader knows that if he wants to he can instantly destroy earth in 0 second with 0 effort), but he's particularly cruel and ensures every death is as agonizing as possible--however, you must not make Godric seemingly drag the fight, he still finishes the annihilation objectively swiftly (undetectably fast to normal mortals as it's infinitely less than a planck second, but but to Godric it's considered as "leisurely slow") but subjective to the opposition an eternity of maximum agony. You must clearly indicate that Godric is using 0% of his power and 0% of effort, and even if Earth is given infinite preparation, all possible advantages, they will still have 0 chance to even tickle Godric or make Godric feel anything. Show Godric be amused by how primitively weak and fragile the earthlings are, how they are trying so hard and effectively doing nothing to him. You must not leave any survivor of Earth alive, serving Godric, living in Thronegate or any other such crap which shows Godric sparing them. Godric’s power must be shown to be absolutely destructive and not give any opposition any possible redemption path.

As usual with Godric, the collaterals must be massive (omniversal scale minimum).

The story must be told from Godric Prime's 3rd person pov (with omniscient narrator if needed), at Year 999...9+, reminiscing about how pathetically weak he was back then compared to how he currently is, and for him to pity his weak self back when he annihilate this universe (highlight the irony and terrifying fact that this subjugation by what he considered to be his weakly pathetic self was already absurdly one-sided and terrifyingly overwhelming--his weak self was effectively using 0% of his power with 0% effort to annihilate that universe, and if that same weak self wasn't in playful mode and wanted to end it instantly, the total annihilation could be done in 0 second. In addition, that weak self destroyed the entire omniverse as collateral. You must make it clear that if the current Godric does it, it will be even more infinitely devastatingly one sided, and he will only be getting unimaginably stronger forever).

You must end the story with the confirmation and dread of how futile the rest of the existence compared to Godric, and that Godric is the most powerful being with unimaginable power growth that dwarfs entire creation, with the rest of the creation trembling in fear of him, and even if the rest from all timelines and from every possible permutations work together to oppose him with unlimited preparation time and resources, they will still fail so completely and won't even make Godric's weakest shield feel the slightest tickle and Godric can completely nonchalantly annihilate them with 0% power and 0% effort in 0 second, and that unfathomable gap will only ever increase infinitely in accelerating manner forever.
