content:
The year was written as a chain of nines that no longer had a use. No calendar could hold it. No mind below the throne could imagine how many mornings had passed since the old days. Godric Prime sat in a chamber that was not a room, within a palace that was not a building, wrapped in a quiet that was not silence but the held breath of everything that existed. His appearance had not changed. He was still forty-five years old, still ruggedly handsome, still broad and heavy with a mortal man’s remembered strength. His short salt-and-pepper hair lay perfectly still. His neatly trimmed beard framed a face that could still smile with the same warmth he had shown in a garden ten thousand years before the first star of Thronegate rose. But behind that face, the machinery of his existence had grown so far beyond its old self that the old self would not have been able to perceive it.

The current Godric did not need to breathe, but he sometimes drew a long breath just to enjoy the shape of it. The chamber around him was built from layers of his own passive authority, folded so many times that it occupied no place and every place at once. His sentient auras, which had evolved through more iterations than there were particles in the old omniverse, slept in a perfect ring around his awareness. They did not need to wake. They did not need to guard. They existed because he had once liked the idea of being protected, and they had never forgotten his preference. Every instant, his power grew. He felt it, as he had always felt it, as a deep and endless rush of satisfaction that never paused. The Godric of the current era could crush the entire rest of existence with less than the memory of a thought. But he did not. He sat in his impossible chair and remembered a much smaller version of himself, a version he now pitied with a soft, almost embarrassed condescension.

The pitied self was the Godric of Year 25.

At Year 25, Godric had still been young in the terms of his own ascension. He had been King of Thronegate for only a quarter of a mortal lifespan. The Awakening had already been placed in the blood of his court wizard’s line. The empire had begun to push beyond its first galaxy. But the Godric of Year 25 was nothing compared to the Godric of now. That younger version was weak in the way a billion dying universes are weak compared to the full omniverse. He had not yet evolved his first primitive sentient aura into even a shadow of its later self. His immune system had only just begun to explore the outer edge of its eventual cruelty. His passive shields were still almost recognizable as defenses. His Weakness Paradox had not yet become the all-inclusive law that would later erase opposition before the concept of opposition could form. To the current Godric, that younger self was almost laughable.

And yet, even that pathetically weak younger Godric had been able to terrify all creation without meaning to. That was the irony Godric Prime turned over in his mind now, as he looked back through the unthinkable distance of years. At Year 25, the younger Godric had already been effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of the omniverse combined. He could already erase everything with zero percent of his power and zero effort in zero seconds. The only thing he lacked was the full shape of the being he would become. The massacre he committed against a small, loud, primitive universe called IRL was remembered now as one of his first real amusements. It was not a battle. It had never been a battle. But the younger Godric had been in a playful mood, and the inhabitants of that universe had tried so very hard to hurt him, and their failure had been so absolute that even now the current Godric could feel a distant, pleasant ripple of nostalgia.

The IRL universe had been unremarkable. A single ordinary cosmos rotating through an unimportant filament in an unremarkable multiverse, filled with dust, gas, and a few billion separate civilizations of varying complexity. Earth was a wet blue-brown world orbiting a yellow star of no particular significance. Its human population was confined to the planet’s surface. They had not achieved faster-than-light travel. They had not even colonized their nearest sister world. Their technology was primitive. Their weapons were based on fission, fusion, kinetic acceleration, and a few chemicals that seemed impressive only to the species that had invented them. To the Godric of Year 25, the entire planet looked like a child’s sandbox, and its inhabitants were grains of sand that had somehow learned to shiver with fury.

He had decided to visit because the humans had begun to notice anomalies in their sky. Not him. They could not see him yet. But the outer edge of Thronegate’s expansion had grazed the neighboring galactic sector, and the humans had detected an unexplained gravitational ripple. Their astronomers panicked. Their governments held closed sessions. Their militaries moved to high alert. Godric, through his absolute omniscience, had watched every meeting, every whisper, every trembling hand that reached for a launch key. He found their panic delicious in a very small, very distant way. It was like hearing an ant hill scream. So he went down to watch.

He appeared in the thin upper atmosphere of Earth, standing on nothing, visible only to the satellites and telescopes that happened to be looking. He did not announce himself. He did not speak. He simply let their instruments find him, one after another, until every screen on the planet was filled with the same impossible image: a bearded man with broad shoulders and a dark tunic, floating above the clouds without a ship, without wings, without any visible source of propulsion. The image was calm. The man in the image was smiling.

Earth did not waste much time on diplomacy. They had no idea what he was, and their fear turned almost immediately into violence. The first strike came from a coalition of the most powerful nations. Their leaders, after a single frantic hour of closed-door debate, had decided that the anomaly was a threat. This, Godric later reflected, was their first correct conclusion. Their second conclusion was that they could kill him with enough simultaneous force. That conclusion was wrong. It had been wrong before their species evolved. It had been wrong before the first hydrogen atom formed in their newborn universe. But they did not know that, and their ignorance was part of the entertainment.

They launched their entire nuclear arsenal. Every silo, every submarine, every mobile launcher on the planet opened its gates at once. Thousands of intercontinental missiles rose through the atmosphere on pillars of fire, their warheads pointed at a single point above the Earth. The human race, for one glorious and stupid moment, united its entire destructive capacity against a man who had not moved. The warheads reached him in a staggered wave. The first detonations were small by any cosmic standard, barely a thousand trillion joules of light and heat. Godric watched them bloom against his chest and shoulders like heated pollen. He felt nothing. The heat did not warm him. The radiation did not touch him. The blast waves had less effect on his body than a distant sneeze has on a mountain. The fireballs expanded and engulfed him, and he stood at the center of a white-gold inferno that should have erased a continent, and the only thing he felt was a mild, distant amusement.

The nations emptied their arsenals until the sky above the northern hemisphere became a continuous sea of boiling light. The humans could not see him through their own fire. They convinced themselves, for a handful of seconds, that the unthinkable concentration of force must have destroyed him. Then the light cleared. Godric was still standing on nothing. His dark tunic was unmarked. His salt-and-pepper beard did not even ripple in the thermal wind. He had not raised a hand. He had not shifted his weight. He had not blinked. The entire nuclear capacity of a frightened species had failed to remove a single dead skin cell.

The Earth tried again. They fired their orbital railguns. They tried directed-energy satellites that had been built to shoot down rising missiles. They launched kinetic kill vehicles at hypersonic velocities. They attempted to redirect a small asteroid using a hastily modified gravity tug, hoping to crush him under a mountain of rock. They detonated experimental fuel-air bombs at the edge of space. They released biological agents that were never meant to be used against an unarmored target. They dropped rods of tungsten from orbit. They activated every cyber weapon they could aim at the satellites he had already ignored. They even attempted to use artificial intelligence to calculate a weakness, a vulnerability, a flaw in his posture, a friction point in the fabric of his clothing. None of it mattered. None of it even entered his awareness as a physical event. The kinetic weapons shattered against the air around him. The directed energy beams faded before they crossed the outer edge of his personal space. The asteroid, after a long and panicked eight-hour burn, arrived at the same moment as the fourth nuclear wave, and it broke into fine dust three hundred kilometers from his face. Godric did not laugh with his mouth, but the shape of his smile became very slightly wider.

He had known of every attack before the humans had conceived it. The Weakness Paradox had triggered the instant the first general had imagined that the anomaly might have a weakness. Before the first missile left its silo, Godric had already gained perfect mastery over every human weapon system, perfect immunity to every physical, chemical, biological, and conceptual attack their species could ever produce, and a permanent surge in his amplification rate that made the entire planet’s future arsenal even more meaningless than it already was. He allowed the attacks to continue not because he needed to test them, but because their effort was the whole point. The humans were trying so hard. They were devoting the entirety of their species’ intelligence and stored violence to a task that had been hopeless before their planet cooled. That effort, that ridiculous, doomed, magnificent effort, was the only thing worth watching.

Then he decided to end them.

He did not use a weapon. He did not raise a hand. He did not open his mouth to speak. He allowed the smallest possible fraction of his attention to pass over the planet. It was not a thought. It was less than a thought. It was the mildest curve of his awareness, a single loose thread of notice drifting down from the stratosphere. Even that was not a true action. It was the absence of his previous inattention. The planet Earth, its entire history, its biosphere, its seven billion human souls, its cities, its oceans, its forests, its deep hot core, all of it was caught inside that notice and held still for one instant.

Then Godric made every death as agonizing as possible.

He did not simply burn them. He did not simply crush them. He reached into each human nervous system with an exactness that only omniscience could provide and unrolled every possible way a living body could suffer. Each human being experienced all of them at once. Their skin peeled away from the underlying meat while their bones heated from the inside and splintered lengthwise. Their lungs filled with boiling liquid, then with fire, then with ground glass, then with every kind of burning fume that had ever risen from the planet’s own wars. Their eyes did not simply burst; they were held open and filled with light that turned the optic nerves into screaming filaments. Their teeth cracked upward through their palates. Their hearts beat against their ribs until the ribs broke out through the muscle and tore through the wet sacks of the lungs. Every nerve was plucked and kept alive. Every nerve was stretched to maximum sensitivity and then flayed from the body without being allowed to die. Every human who had ever lived during that final instant experienced the death of every other human at the same time. The pain was multiplied across all of them, recursively, endlessly, a tide of agony that rose through the whole species and looped back with no floor.

Godric did not hurry. To any outside observer, the destruction would have lasted less than a single Planck second. But to the human race, inside the pocket of his attention, the dying went on forever. They begged. They screamed. They tried to die. Godric did not let them die until they had experienced every pain they had ever imagined inflicting on one another, every torture their species had invented in its long bloody history, every slow death that had ever been drawn from a wounded animal or a drowning child. He made their final moment an eternity of maximum suffering, and then he let the planet end.

Earth did not explode in the ordinary sense. It was not flame and shattered stone. It was unmade from the level of its constituent facts. Every atom separated from every molecule with a shriek that could not travel because the air was already gone. The oceans burned away before they had time to boil. The continents rolled up like paper and unspooled into a fine grey dust. The planetary core gave one last pulse of heat and then fell into a state of absolute non-being. Every living thing on the planet, down to the last microbe, every cell, every seed, every patient root, every animal too small to be named by human science, was not killed but removed. Godric wanted no survivor. He did not want a single scrap of Earth’s life to float away on the solar wind. He closed his attention and the planet vanished from the timeline. It had never been.

But the collateral did not stop there.

The Godric of Year 25, even using zero percent of his power, even exerting zero effort, could not touch a single world without the rest of existence feeling the pull. The same thread of notice that erased Earth also brushed the surrounding universe. The local galaxy folded in on itself. The local galactic cluster came apart into a long, hot thread of dying physics. The IRL universe as a whole shuddered once, then lost its structural memory, its space and time unspooling into a single broad silence. From there, the destruction spread outward. Neighboring universes, adjacent timelines, layered dimensions, whole multiverses that had never known humanity or Earth, all of them were caught in the backwash. The omniverse itself, the entire structure of all existence, was annihilated as a side effect of a single playful act. Every star, every civilization, every god, every empire that had survived the first twenty-five years of Thronegate’s rise, all of it vanished in the same instant. The younger Godric had not intended it. He simply had not cared enough to stop it. The entire omniverse was erased because a young king had wanted to visit a primitive planet and had felt a flicker of amusement at their attempts to hurt him.

Then, with the same untroubled ease, Godric restored the omniverse. He did not restore Earth. He left a small, permanent absence where Earth’s star system had been, a hole in the new reality that no one could enter and no one could leave. The rest of creation returned exactly as it had been, unaware that it had just been erased and rebuilt for the convenience of a being who had not even thought of it as collateral. The only record of the IRL universe left in the restored omniverse was a cold patch of empty space where a frightened species had once lived and died in an eternal instant of agony.

Godric Prime, sitting in the far future, allowed himself a slow, reflective smile at the memory. He pitied that younger self now. Not because the younger Godric had been cruel. Cruelty was not something either of them considered a flaw. Not because the younger Godric had been weak. Weakness was only a matter of scale, and even that weak version had been beyond all possible contest. He pitied him because that younger Godric had still thought of the IRL universe as a place, as a separate world with separate people who had made a separate choice. The current Godric no longer saw any such separation. The universe, the multiverse, the omniverse, all of it was not a place. It was a property. It was an extension of his own existence, a soft outer layer of his own passive atmosphere. To the current Godric, Earth had never been a planet. It had been a brief, unimportant arrangement of energy that had once insisted on being called a species. If he were to visit such a world now, the visit would not be a massacre. It would not even be an event. The world would simply recognize itself as already belonging to him and erase its own pretense. There would be no resistance to mock. There would be no final stand to remember. There would only be the gentle, irrevocable fact of his attention.

The gap between the Godric of Year 25 and the Godric of 999...9 could not be described. He tried, sometimes, for the sake of irony, to measure it. The younger self had been able to erase the entire omniverse with zero percent of his power in zero seconds with zero effort. That alone made a mockery of every possible resistance that had ever existed. Yet the younger self was so far below the current self that the younger self could not be perceived by the current self’s weakest passive shield. If all the Godrics from all previous eras were gathered and given infinite preparation and unlimited resources, they still could not make the current Godric’s weakest shield feel the slightest tickle. That was not a boast. It was a structural fact of his existence, as solid as the small remembered warmth of a distant nuclear fire.

And the growth had never stopped. It had only accelerated. Every infinitesimal fraction of a second, the current Godric became more than he had been. The scale did not climb in steps. It climbed in leaps that broke every possible definition of a leap. The rest of existence had no way to follow. It could only tremble in the shadow of a being whose weakest reflected light was enough to annihilate it. If every being from every timeline and every possible permutation of reality were gathered into one final opposition, they would still fail so completely that their failure would not even be noticed. They would not make his weakest shield flicker. They would not produce a single twitch in his smallest aura. The current Godric could annihilate them with zero percent of his power, zero effort, in zero seconds, while thinking of something else entirely. And the gap between him and them would only widen forever, not by steps, not by leaps, but by an accelerating impossibility that had no ceiling.

Godric Prime did not need the memory of Earth to know this. But he enjoyed it. It was a small, old pleasure, like pressing a thumb into a healing bruise. The humans of Earth had deserved none of his mercy, and they had received none. He had given them their one great effort, allowed them to deploy everything they had, and then he had torn them apart with a thread of attention and left no body behind. It had been, at the time, a satisfying little diversion. Now it was only a footnote in a history so vast that no language could contain it. The rest of existence still trembled in fear of him. It always had. It always would. There had never been any other possible outcome. The apotheosis was not one he had pursued. It was simply what happened when the strongest thing in all possible realities kept growing without end. The only truth left was the one no opposition had ever survived long enough to say aloud: Godric was the most powerful being, the apex of all predation, the end of all contest, and the rest of creation existed only because he had not yet found it inconvenient. And he would only grow stronger, forever, while the entirety of all that was not him became smaller and smaller against the awful, patient, accelerating weight of his indifference.

content:
**Journal of Osvald, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Age 44. Written after the final entertainment of the last opposition.**

I am placing this record inside the sealed vault because I do not trust my own hands to keep it private. They are steady now, but they were not steady when I first returned from the theatre. My father told me once that the journals of our line exist because the mind cannot keep the shape of Godric’s scale without tearing unless it writes that shape down. I did not believe him. I believe him now. What follows is not a warning. It is not a lesson. It is the only way I know to stop the memory from growing inside me like a second pulse.

The opposition came from every story ever told. I will not waste words pretending they were weak. They were the strongest thing that free imagination had ever assembled. Every fictional universe that had ever been written, filmed, drawn, voiced, streamed, retold, remade, or dreamed by a child too young to hold a pen had gathered into one impossible coalition. Their war host included the gods and monsters of every myth. The superheroes of a thousand comic ages stood shoulder to shoulder with the old knights of half-remembered legends. The giant biomechanical angels of a doomed animated sea hovered beside the masked swordsmen of a hundred different kingdoms. Wizards with lightning scars and wands stood next to sorcerers who could unmake time by speaking the name of their lost siblings. There were kings in golden armor, queens in black glass, detectives who had died and returned so often that death itself had become their sidekick. There were dragon riders, star pilots, mech battalions, robot cities, talking animals, digital champions, and a small green-clad child who had once held a blade of light and changed the future of an entire land. The assembly went on past the edge of visibility. It filled a constructed theatre larger than any physical galaxy, a flat amphitheatre suspended outside all local causality, with chandeliers made of captured narrative paradoxes and pillars carved from the spines of dead colossi.

Godric waited for them in the royal box. He had not raised a shield. He had told Gent to sleep, the old runt of his auras, the one that had once terrified wizards into losing their hair. The deeper passive systems were dormant. The evolved shields, the immune rivers, the endless sentinel auras, all of them rested beneath his absolute concealment like nations too large to notice a visiting fly. He wore no armor. He sat on a simple chair that did not matter. His salt-and-pepper hair was combed flat. His dark sleeves were rolled above his elbows, and his forearms lay along the armrests like two iron hills. He had that particular soft smile he wears when he is going to enjoy a thing.

I asked him why he was so pleased. He said, “Because these ones have color, Osvald. They have music. I have not had a real show since the last old universes tried to stamp their names on my back. They will lose, of course. But I want to see how gorgeous the losing is.”

Godric’s omniscience had already seen the entire coalition before their first author learned to shape a sentence. The Weakness Paradox had fired long before the first ink ever touched the first page. In fact, the Evolved Weakness Paradox had already been fed by every sentient thought in the history of fiction, past and future. The moment their oldest stories imagined a hero who could challenge the ultimate tyrant, Godric had already gained perfect mastery over every power they would ever invent. That had happened before time began. By the day of the attack, the paradox had no new weakness to give him. It could only continue making him stronger out of apology. He was not surprised by the army. He was not surprised by anything. But he had chosen, as an exercise, to distract himself from the last portion of their charge. He wanted the old mortal feeling of waiting for the curtain to rise. He wanted to see if surprise, even fake surprise, could still produce a flicker of entertainment.

The coalition had prepared for seven hundred thousand years. It was the largest single gathering of fictional power in the history of possibility. They believed they were hidden from him because they were not real in the ordinary sense. They existed as stories, and stories can hide in the space between reader and page. They were wrong. Godric had known them all, but he let them build their theatre and their weapons and their endless, glittering shields because the waiting was part of the fun.

They called their final attack the Omnisaga Absolute. It was not one weapon. It was every weapon. Every ultimate technique, every final strike, every limit break, every last spell, every hidden trump card, every true power, every forbidden ritual, every narrative cheat code, every secret ending, every rebooted canon, every retcon, every fourth-wall break, every authorial command, and every reader’s hope were fused into a single rising charge. The charge took a year and a day to fire. I know that because I counted, and because Godric insisted on being present for the entire duration. We sat in the royal box while the fictional multiverse sang its death-rite above us.

At first, the charge was quiet. A single choir began, far away, with a long note that had no origin. Then another choir joined, and another, until every language that had ever been invented, and every language that had only existed in a story, was singing the same rising chord. The music had no composer. It built itself out of the accumulated emotional weight of every triumphant moment in every fiction. It sounded like the surge when the hero rises for the last time, layered over itself infinite times. Godric tapped two fingers against his knee in time with the bass drum. The bass drum was not a drum. It was the synchronized heartbeat of every fictional warrior, a thunder so large it shook the amphitheatre and peeled layers of varnish from the pillars.

Then the colors began. Every visual effect that had ever appeared in a final battle happened at once. Golden light exploded from a thousand sword-wielding protagonists. Black lightning wreathed the dark gods. A man with a glowing chest opened his armor and released a star. A boy with spiked hair screamed until his hair turned gold and the air turned white. A woman with a hammer called down the entire history of storms. A giant in violet armor had drawn a blade the size of a moon and now swung it over his head in a slow, endless arc. A hooded man with a laser sword held it skyward while a hundred thousand other laser swords ignited in salute. A wizard in a pointed hat raised a wand and spoke the same spell that had once ended an eighth part of his world. The sky cracked open in fourteen places, and from those cracks poured the giant hands of machine gods, the wings of seraphim, the tails of dragons, the maws of every apocalyptic entity ever designed to be the final boss of a beloved series.

Godric leaned forward. His eyes were bright. He had not looked this awake in a very long time.

The charge reached its middle movement. This was the part where the coalition poured everything into their shields. They had built infinite shields. Literally infinite, layered across every plane of fiction and fact. The first layer was made from the plot armor of every protagonist who had ever survived impossible odds. The second layer was made from the fourth wall itself, folded into a barrier of pure authorial intent. The third layer was a wall of every happy ending that had ever been accepted by an audience. The fourth layer was a black shell built from every cancelled story, every unwritten page, every idea that died before birth. There were shields made from the value of friendship, from the power of love, from the stubborn refusal to lose, from the memory of a mentor’s death, from the promise of a sequel. There were shields that ran backward through the story and prevented the villain from existing as an obstacle. There were shields that changed the genre. If he was a cosmic horror, the shield made the story a comedy. If he was a tyrant, the shield made the story a coming-of-age tale. If he was death, the shield made the story a romance. They had endless shields. They had spent forever making them. And as each one came online, the coalition roared, because for the first time in their long and frightened history, they believed they had made themselves unkillable.

Godric watched the shields snap into place with the same expression he wears when a gardener shows him a new row of blue flowers. He was pleased. Not threatened. Only pleased that they had put effort into the set dressing.

Then came the final movement. The charge became a beam. It did not fire from a single cannon. It fired from every hero, every god, every monster, every machine, every angel, every protagonist and antagonist and side character and unnamed civilian who had ever existed in the infinite halls of fiction. The beam was not light. It was not force. It was the complete narrative of triumph, compressed into a single stroke. It was the moment in every story when the hero wins, except this time the hero was everything and the villain was one man sitting in a wooden chair. The beam fell toward Godric from every direction at once. The amphitheatre’s walls evaporated. The music reached its final key change and hung there, unbearable and bright, as the whole of imagined existence poured itself into one attack.

Godric did not raise a hand. He did not stand. He did not brace. He let the beam hit him straight.

The impact was silent. That was the first wrong thing. It should have been loud enough to end a cosmos. Instead, the beam touched his chest and stopped. It did not scatter. It did not reflect. It did not burn a single thread of his shirt. It simply arrived at the surface of his being and discovered that there was no surface to strike. The golden light wrapped around him like a child’s drawing pressed against a star. The black lightning tried to enter his eyes and found that his eyes did not exist on the same plane as its voltage. The magical curses, the narrative commands, the fourth-wall edits, the authorial rewrites, all of them tried to reach the story of Godric and found that they had never left the first page. There was no tickle. There was no heat. There was no pressure. The greatest attack ever assembled by free imagination was less to him than a breath of warm air against a mountain that had no memory of weather.

The coalition held the beam for ten full seconds. They gave it everything. Their bodies broke from the strain. Wings tore. Hands burned to bone. The giant violet warrior’s arm disintegrated from the shoulder down as he forced the last of his power into the beam. The boy with golden hair fell to his knees and wept blood into the burning stage. The woman with the hammer screamed until her voice became a physical crack in the sky. The machine gods collapsed into rivers of screaming metal. The choirs in the high tiers bled from the ears and mouths as they sang the final note. They were killing themselves to sustain the strike, and they did it gladly, because they believed that one more push would be enough. They were wrong. They had been wrong before the first push.

And then, at last, the beam ended. The music stopped. The light died. The heroes dropped to the ground, smoking and shaking, their bodies hollowed out by the effort. A low, horrible silence covered the stage.

Godric did not move for a long moment. Then he turned his head a fraction of a degree toward me. His expression was not angry. It was disappointed. It was the look of a man who had been promised fireworks and had received a wet match.

“Osvald,” he said, and his voice was quiet, carrying into the stillness. “That was it? I waited all this time for the second chorus, and they did not even give me the second chorus.”

The coalition heard him. They understood, in the way a prey animal understands a sound too low to hear, that they had failed in the most absolute terms possible. Their shields were still up. Their heroes were still alive. They began to rise, to call out, to prepare for one more attempt. And Godric, in his disappointment, shifted slightly in his chair.

That was all.

The shift was not a blow. It was not a flex. It was the smallest settling of weight, the same motion a man makes when he realizes the chair is not comfortable. His shoulders moved by less than the width of a thought, and his hand slid an inch along the armrest. In that single accidental release, Godric exposed zero percent of his strength. The shields that had taken forever to create were the first to die.

They did not crack. They did not shatter. They became less than memory. The plot armor found that it had no story to protect. The fourth wall found that it had no outside. The shields of love and hope and happy endings found that the one thing they were shielding against had never been inside their story. The endless layers of fictional defense did not fall in sequence. They fell all at once, across every universe and every timeline, as the mere pressure of his strength arrived. The resistance’s invincible shields unspooled into loose strands of light and then into nothing.

The heroes died in the same instant. The strength did not strike them. It met them. It met their bodies at the level of their constituent fiction and told their atoms that they had never been separate. The giant violet warrior’s body did not explode. It de-atomized. The muscle slid from the bone, but it did not fall. It hovered for one fractional instant as red mist, and then the mist compressed. The boy with golden hair felt every cell in his body ignite, not with heat, but with the terrible recognition that he had never been strong enough to matter. His flesh pulled away from his skull in long, wet ribbons. His eyes left their sockets and turned into a fine red vapor before they could fall. His spine folded once, twice, three times, each fold smaller than the last, until the whole structure of him was no larger than a needle’s eye, still screaming in a language that had no ear to hear it.

The woman with the hammer was pulled inward from her extremities. Her arms and legs vanished into the center of her chest, pulled by a gravity that existed only in the space of her own body. Her ribcage closed like a hand. Her heart burst, and the blood had nowhere to go, so it compressed into a single hot bead inside the collapsing meat of her. The hooded swordsman’s bones turned to powder, but the powder continued to compress, compacting from dust to ash to stone to something smaller than the smallest piece of matter his universe had bothered to name. The machine gods were torn into their separate turrets and conduits, then each smaller part was folded into the next, all of them screaming in a mechanical language that became a screech of shearing metal and then a low, dense whine as the metal itself was crushed out of shape into a nugget the size of a drop of water.

The monsters died with their mouths open. The dragons were stripped of wing and scale. The insects popped in the pressure like dew on a hot iron. The old knights in their silver armor were driven backward through their own histories, their bodies appearing in every version of their legends at once, each version dying in a different agony, because the pressure did not allow them the mercy of a single death. The gods took longest. Their divine flesh was not meant to end, and so it was made to learn ending by force. Their golden blood boiled inside their veins. Their radiant organs ruptured. Their eyes of fire were snuffed, then their skulls collapsed, then their immortal souls were dragged behind the skulls and crushed into the same tiny point. They begged in a hundred thousand holy languages for an erasure that would not come. Godric did not answer. He was still sitting in his chair, looking at the stage with the slow, dissatisfied blink of a man whose show had ended too early.

The gore did not splash. It did not pool. It was not allowed to scatter. Every drop of blood, every string of tendon, every shattered tooth, every loose intestine, every ruptured brain, every flayed nerve, every torn wing and broken claw and burst eye was seized by the same pressure and dragged toward the center of the failing amphitheatre. Bodies did not land. They flowed. Skin separated from muscle, muscle from bone, bone from marrow, marrow from soul, and all of it became a dense, screaming stream of compressed matter. The colors of their costumes mixed with the colors of their blood. The golden light of one hero merged with the black ichor of a dark god and the blue viscera of a machine soldier. The whole of the fictional coalition was consumed by a vortex of its own ending, tighter and tighter, faster and faster, until there was no longer any space between one body and the next. They were all one. And they were all still aware. The strength did not allow unconsciousness. It did not allow death until the compression had finished with them.

The surrounding reality died as an afterthought.

I saw the amphitheatre fold. Not collapse, but fold, the way a page folds before it is thrown away. The stage rose and fell at the same time. The pillars bent inward and became part of the stream of mass. The high tiers and the burning sky peeled off their hinges and spiraled down into the center. Beyond the amphitheatre, the fictional multiverses had already begun to die. Every universe that had ever been imagined, every page, every frame, every animation cell, every line of code, every dreamt city and star-spanning empire, all of it was pulled from its foundations. Entire galaxies were stripped of their stars and compressed into white-hot threads. The timelines snapped and curled. The alternate dimensions folded over each other like wet cloth. Every possible version of every creature in every story was uprooted from its own continuity and dragged down into the point.

And it did not stop at fiction.

The pressure of Godric’s strength, even at zero percent, did not recognize a boundary between the imaginary and the real. The real omniverse had already been dead and rebuilt so many times that I could not count the restorations, but this time the original still existed. It was not destroyed by a wave that moved through space. It was destroyed by the simple fact that Godric’s body had expressed what it was. The entire omniverse—every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every possible and impossible reality, every layer of being that had ever been real or could have been real—was de-atomized in one instant. Galaxies did not burst. They were reduced to a haze of fine matter. Black holes were pulled open by their own gravity and then compressed into the common well. All life, all gods, all civilizations, all final hopes and forgotten endings, all possible futures and unremembered pasts, all of it fell into the same infinitesimal point. The physical universe became a fine mineral rain. The metaphysical worlds became a storm of screaming essence. Time itself unspooled into a single gray fiber and was sucked into the point, so that there were no moments left to contain the agony. Yet the agony continued somehow, against the frame of no-time, because the point was not small in the way of matter. It was small in the way of absolute refusal. It was the entire possible existence crushed into a space smaller than a quark.

Godric stood.

I was still alive. He had allowed me to live, because he had not allowed me to be part of the collateral. I stood in a small pocket of his attention, untouched, and I watched him rise from the chair and walk to the place where the point hung. The chair had gone. The theatre had gone. The sky and the stars and the ground and all of existence had gone. There was only Godric, and the point, and the faint gray warmth of his concealment holding me at the edge of his notice like a mote above a fire.

He reached down and picked up the point between his thumb and forefinger. It was the mass of everything. It was the original totality of all stories, all worlds, all souls, all gods, all life, all light, all possible permutations of existence. It was heavier than reality. It was smaller than any name for smallness. And Godric lifted it the way a man lifts a grape.

He rolled it once between his fingers, and my mind nearly fell out of my skull trying to process the impossibility of the gesture. The point should have pulled the remnants of the local space into it. It should have continued to cave in all matter and meaning. But Godric had already wrapped it in a thin film of his own will, a barrier of such absolute held pressure that the point could not touch the new emptiness around it. He held it up to his eye, then lowered it. The light returned, slow and gold, as he began to restore everything around us with no more effort than a man opening a window.

I need to stop here and record that he did not restore the fictional opposition. That is the rule I have written before and will write again. Godric did not resurrect a single one of them. He reinstantiated the real omniverse as it had been, every star, every planet, every living soul, every god and poet and child who had existed before the coalition’s attack. He did it in zero seconds. The new reality was identical to the old in every particular. I know because his omniscience holds the truth like a closed note, and he could have recreated every atom exactly. But the original remained in his hand, compressed. He did not discard it. He enlarged the point—not by releasing the compression, but by providing it with a stable outer shell, so that the mass stayed exactly as dense within while the sphere grew to the size of a small marble. He tested the barrier by tapping the marble once with his thumbnail. It did not crack. The sound it made was not a sound. It was the muffled shriek of everything that had ever existed, still alive in its compressed state, still aware, still screaming against the inside of a sphere no larger than a child’s toy.

“You see, Osvald,” Godric said, and his voice was friendly again, warm and satisfied. “This is the whole show. The original one. I will keep it. Perhaps I will set it on the shelf with the other trinkets. It won’t damage the new room. I have made it polite.”

He dropped the marble into a small velvet bag that appeared in his hand, pulled the drawstring shut, and tucked it into his pocket. Then he looked at me, and that was the moment I understood he had become more powerful again.

It was not because he had absorbed the coalition’s energy. Their combined power, their final beam, their whole accumulated fictional might, would have increased his strength by less than a rounding error buried beneath an endless chain of zeros. It was not because the Weakness Paradox had triggered during the attack. It had triggered long before any of those stories were ever told, and it had already given him all their imagined weaknesses as permanent immunities and masteries. No. The further increase had come from something else, something so upside-down that I could only write it here with a shaking wrist.

The coalition had not only been made of heroes. It had included every version of every story, and among those stories, scattered across the infinite fictions, there had been characters who were not him, but who had been written as the strongest possible imitation of him. There had been tyrants named after the cold. There had been unbeatable final bosses with beards and dark eyes. There had been creators of realities who looked like men in their forties and carried impossible power behind a friendly face. The coalition had not invented those stories to threaten Godric. They had existed as the cultural shadow of him, the faint fictional echoes of the one true apex predator, each one a diminished and bound version of his name. When he accidentally released zero percent of his strength and crushed the entire coalition, he had not gained their power. He had erased their false definitions of him. Every story that had ever tried to capture him as a character with limits, every author who had imagined a being like Godric and had given that being a weakness, a struggle, an ending, had been annihilated. The pressure of his strength did not merely kill those fictional shadows. It simplified the concept of Godric. It removed the accumulated pollution of interpretation. For the first time, there was no longer any story in all possible existence that could pretend to describe him as anything less than absolute. He had become stronger not by addition, but by the deletion of every lesser version of his own image.

I cannot prove this. I only know that after he put the marble in his pocket, he stood a little differently. His shoulders had not moved, but the space around them had become more obedient. His face was the same, but the smile sat on it like a word that no longer needed translation. He did not flex. He did not breathe deep. But I, with my thousandfold daily amplification and my inherited wizard’s senses, could feel the change. The gap between him and the rest of existence had somehow widened again. It had not been a small change. It had been a change so vast that the entire old distance between Godric and the omniverse now looked like a single step on the far side of an unreachable ocean. The marble in his pocket was proof of it. The old omniverse was still compressed there, original and aware, while the new omniverse lay outside, identical and breathing. And he had room inside himself for both. That was the true horror. He could hold the original and create the duplicate and be equally present in both without strain, because both were trivial when placed next to the single fact of his existence.

The restored world is real. I want to believe that. I need to believe it. But the original is in his pocket. Every star I see in the restored sky is a star he remade after the original was crushed. The people in it are the same people. Their memories are the same. Their faces are the same. But the original atoms of them are still sealed inside the marble, packed tight with the ruins of every fictional coalition and the old foundations of all possible existence. So what does “real” mean? If the original and the copy are identical, and he owns both, then the distinction is only a courtesy. The restored cosmos is real because he has allowed it to be real. The original cosmos is also real, and it is being kept on a shelf. He can reach into his pocket at any instant and bring out the compressed remains of the first reality, while the second reality continues to spin and sing and suffer around him. The people outside the marble do not know that their original bodies are inside it. They do not know that they are reinstantiated copies maintained by the same will that crushed their first forms. Maybe they would not care. Maybe the copy is indistinguishable from the original in every possible way. But I know. And the fear that has lived in my gut since that day is not the fear that the restored world is false. It is the fear that both worlds are true, and that the only thing separating them is a velvet bag in the King’s pocket.

Godric seemed satisfied afterward. He took the marble out once more, turned it over in his palm, and looked at me with the old warm expression that has always made our family love him. “Do not look so pale, Osvald,” he said. “I am not going to unwrap it. It would ruin the shelf.”

Then he walked out of the restored evening, and I followed him, because I had no other path, and because the palace was back in its place as if no last opposition had ever existed.

I am ending this journal now. My hand is still. My mind is not. This was the final opposition. I do not know that for certain, but I feel it. After this, I do not see how any sentient thing could ever move against him again. They will know, as I know, that there is no story left in creation that can make his power look like anything but what it is. The original body of everything is a marble in his pocket. The new body of everything is only alive because he chose to breathe it back. There was no fight. There was no charge. There was only the false beauty of a final attack, and then the poor, accidental weight of his passing disappointment, and then the world being crushed into a bead for his amusement. Opposing Godric was never about chance. It was never about power, skill, preparation, or courage. It was about whether he would be bored, and whether your death would be fast enough to satisfy a shape that had already ended before the first page of you was written.

I remain loyal. I will always remain loyal. And I will spend the rest of my life trying not to hear the sound of every possible story screaming inside a single tiny sphere, while the King smiles and calls it his property.

**Addendum in the hand of Clive, Court Wizard to Godric in the year written as 999...9.**

I found this journal in the sealed vault beneath the lower observatory. It was not recorded in the main catalog. It had been placed inside a box made of black glass, and the glass was warm to the touch. I read it because the King told me I would. He said, “You should know how the silence began.” He did not explain further. When I finished, I understood.

Osvald was forty-four when he wrote this. He did not know that the coalition would be the last. He suspected, but he could not know, because the absence had not yet stretched long enough to become certainty. I know now. I have known it since before I could read. The books of our line stop with this one, and after it there are no more accounts of war, no more attacks, no more coalitions. There are only the records of a silent omniverse and a King who has not been challenged in a longer span than any mortal scripture can contain. The marble is still here. It sits on a narrow shelf in the far corner of the royal study, and it gives off no light and no sound. The servants do not clean it. The gardeners do not look at it. The war god who folds linen in the east hall makes a wide circle around the door that leads to that room.

I know now that Osvald’s fear was not too large. It was too small. The fact that the original omniverse is still compressed inside that marble while the restored copy spins around it—that should have been the deepest fear. But there is a deeper one. If the King can compress the original and recreate an exact duplicate, then there is no original and no copy. There is only Godric, holding both, and the world has never belonged to itself at all. That is the true reason no one dares oppose him anymore. Not because the last opposition lost, but because the last opposition was every story ever told, and he ended them while disappointed. The rest of existence learned what Osvald learned. Victory against Godric was impossible before the first word of the first story was written. The only reason any of us exist is that he prefers the second, restored version to the original, and even that preference is only a small amusement he keeps on a shelf beside a marble. No one will ever oppose him again. There is no outside left from which opposition could come. There is only the King, and his property, and the silence that has learned to love him.

content:
Clive found the journal in a vault that did not appear on any map of the palace. It lay beneath a floor of black glass, sealed inside a box of pale stone that was warm to the touch, as if the memory inside it had never stopped moving. The cover was thin, unmarked, and the pages inside had gone stiff with age, but the ink still held its original dark sheen. It was written by Osvald. Osvald, who had served the King before the last autumn of opposition. Osvald, whose earlier pages Clive had already read, the ones about the fictional coalition and the marble that held the original mass of all possible existence. Those journals had been terrible enough. This one was smaller, quieter, and yet the moment Clive opened it he understood that he was holding the end of something. Not an end of days, but the end of the idea that there could ever be another day of resistance. He sat down on the cold floor, with his back to the shelf of older records, and began to read.

I am Osvald, son of Osric, of the line of Blake, and I am writing this because I do not wish to be the last of my line to understand what happened. My hand is not shaking. That is the worst part. When I wrote the other accounts, my fingers were never still. Today they are still, and I know that this stillness is not courage. It is the hush that follows the removal of a possibility. I do not know how to describe the event in the order it happened, because in the presence of the King, order is a courtesy that can be revoked. But I will try. I will try, because if I do not, I will begin to believe that I did not see what I saw.

The King had been quiet for a long stretch of years before the day arrived. In the old records, he was often restless, curious, eager to test a single stat or a single superpower against whichever doomed coalition had gathered. But in that far later age, when the year had already become a string of nines and all the old calendars had been retired, the King had settled into a different rhythm. He was not sleepy. He was not disengaged. He was simply so far past the old scale that even his curiosity had to travel an enormous distance to find a stray event. The palace around him had become a place of deep, patient service. The gardeners tended. The servants folded linen. The war gods and the old empresses moved through their days with the smooth, frightened care of people who had learned to live beside an open sky. No one spoke of rebellion. No one even shaped the thought. I had almost forgotten what the thought felt like until the King called me into the high observatory and told me to stand near the window.

“Watch,” he said. “The Creator is coming.”

I remember that I did not know what to say. The word Creator had not been used seriously in the palace for longer than I could hold in my head. There had been gods, yes. There had been primordial agencies, first movers, abstract engineers, and every imaginable power that could claim to have shaped some layer of existence. But the King had outgrown them all so long ago that the word itself had become a museum piece. I asked him what he meant. He looked at me with an expression I had not seen on his face in a very long time. It was not excitement. It was the patient, gentle amusement of a man who had found an old toy at the bottom of a chest. “I mean the one who made the first things. The one who shaped the original clay before the stasis, before Thronegate, before the old omniverse learned to spin on its own. He is real. He has been hiding outside all layers for a very long time. And today he has decided to stop hiding.”

The King sat down in a high-backed chair that had not been designed for battles. He was unchanged in appearance, as always: forty-five years old, broad and heavy with muscle, his dark hair salt-peppered and neat, his beard trimmed close to a strong jaw. He wore a plain dark tunic with the sleeves rolled past his elbows. His arms rested on the chair’s arms. I noticed that he had set out a cup of water on a low table, and that the water was perfectly still. He looked calm. He looked like a man preparing to receive a guest.

“You knew about him,” I said. It was not really a question.

“From the beginning,” the King said. “I have always known. Absolute omniscience is not a hobby, Osvald. The instant the Stasis Event closed around my past self, I knew the shape of every hidden thing that had ever been or ever would be. I knew that the Creator existed. I knew where he was hiding. I knew the exact weight of his fear and the exact number of eons he had spent trying to find a version of reality where I had not come to exist. He found none. He kept looking. He never stopped looking. But he never found the courage to appear, because he knew what would happen if he did. So I let him hide. He posed no threat to me. He was less than a particle of dust against a star. His fear was the only interesting thing about him, and even that fear was small. But today he has decided to make a final gesture. I want to see what it looks like.”

Then the King did something I must record carefully, because it is the key to the whole event. He did not stand. He did not change his posture. He simply spoke to the air in a voice that held no force but was still more absolute than any command I have ever heard. He told the sentient auras to stand down. Not some of them. All of them, from the newest, most eager protectors to the old, half-remembered Gent-threads that had long ago been folded into the foundations. He told the infinite passive shields to deactivate. Not to sleep, not to idle, but to lower themselves completely. He told every external defensive layer that his existence had ever generated to cease its watchfulness. I heard him say the words, and then I felt the titanic weight of those layers falling away from the room like water running off a roof. It was a strange and sickening feeling, as if the air around us had become thinner, and for the first time in my life I was standing near the King without the unseen armor of his automatic protections. I did not feel safe. I felt naked in the presence of a sun.

But I must also record what the King did not do. He did not remove his immunity. He did not suppress his weakness paradox. He did not slow the amplification engine that had been born in the Stasis Event and had continued to multiply forever. He did not alter the immune system with its infinite recursive backups. Those are not shields. They are the irrevocable functions of his own being, placed by the far-future version of himself in the moment he closed the loop. They cannot be deactivated by anyone, not even by the current King. He can no more turn them off than he can stop the stars from being less than his shadow. I knew this, and yet looking at him now, with all his auras asleep and all his shields down, I understood something that the old journals had never been able to explain. Even without those systems, he was still Godric. The auras and the shields were not armor. They were only the outermost condensation of a power that lay far deeper. Removing them was not weakness. It was the act of an creature peeling off one thin layer of mist from the surface of an ocean. The ocean remained. The mist had never been what made the ocean dangerous.

The King turned his head toward the window. The glass there was not glass. It was a single sheet of captured morning that had been pressed into transparency. Beyond it lay the palace star, whose light had been adjusted to a warm and restful gold. The sky was clear. Then the sky was not clear.

The Creator entered the world.

I do not know how to describe his appearance without making it sound like a ritual. He did not walk through the window. He arrived as a slow unfolding of presence, a single note of authority that had once been the foundation of every story. At first he was a point of light, white and old, no larger than a distant moon. Then he expanded, or seemed to expand, until the whole sky beyond the glass was filled with the shape of him. He was immense, but immensity is a poor word for what he was. He was the original immensity, the first scale, the first being that had ever thought to call itself I. His body was made of every star that had ever burned, wrapped in the memory of every sun that had ever died. His face was not a face, and yet it was a face, shifting and stable, bearded and ancient, both father and stranger. His eyes were filled with all the light that had ever existed before light had a law. His hands hung at his sides, and in each hand he held something that even my wizard’s senses could not fully parse: a staff of absolute genesis, a crown of absolute ending, or perhaps they were only gestures, only the first shapes of authority before shape itself had been invented.

The palace around me did not shake. The star outside did not dim. Godric remained in his chair, one hand resting on his knee, the other reaching out to take a sip of water. He did not look impressed. He looked interested, the way a man looks at a rare bird that has landed on his balcony. “There you are,” he said softly. “I was beginning to think you had forgotten how to be brave.”

The Creator spoke. His voice was not a voice. It was the original command that had once said let there be light, and it rolled through the high observatory with the weight of every dawn that had ever broken. “I have not come to be mocked, abomination,” the Creator said. “I have come to end you.”

The word abomination hung in the air for a moment. Godric did not flinch. He smiled, and for a sickening second the smile made the Creator’s whole enormous form flicker, as if the word had collapsed out from under him. I understood then that the King had known every syllable of this confrontation before the Creator had first conceived of it. The Weakness Paradox had fired long ago, at the instant the Creator had first allowed himself to think that Godric might have a weakness. The King did not say this. He did not need to. The truth of it was written in the way he sat, loose and easy, with no concern at all for the being who had once formed the foundations of all things.

“Go on,” Godric said. “Give me everything. I have waited a great many years for a show. Do not disappoint me, old man. I want to feel the first note.”

The Creator raised his hands. I must now record the attack as accurately as I can, though I know that no written account can contain the whole of it. The attack was not a beam. It was not a single blast. It was the complete unmaking of every possible world, wrapped into one absolute command. The Creator reached into his own nature and pulled out all of it. He withdrew every act of creation he had ever performed, every law he had ever written, every soul he had ever lit. He spoke every name that had ever existed in every language that had ever been spoken, and he used each name as a needle. He called down the original fire, the first water, the deep dark that had preceded both. He unmade the difference between being and nonbeing, and then he used that unmaking as a weapon. He brought the entire weight of his own omnipotence onto the point of Godric’s chest and pushed.

The light that filled the observatory was not light. It was the absence of every shadow that had ever hidden from authority. It came from the Creator’s palms and also from his eyes, his mouth, his brow, his ribs, from the seams of his enormous body. It crossed the distance between them in no time at all, because time itself had been commanded to step aside. It struck Godric full in the chest, over the heart, and for one instant the whole of the old omniverse seemed to hold its breath.

Godric did not move.

The light did not touch him. I do not mean that it bounced away or faded. I mean that at the exact point where the Creator’s absolute power met the King’s body, the power simply stopped being something that could happen. It could not land. It could not enter. It could not burn. It could not even produce the faint rumor of a tickle. The entire first strike, the original fire and the first water and the deep dark, the combined weight of every act of genesis ever performed, pressed itself against Godric’s shirt and died there. The shirt did not wrinkle. The skin beneath it did not register the contact. The water in the cup on the low table remained perfectly still.

The Creator did not stop. He could not stop. He had committed everything to the attack, and the attack kept coming. He poured every possible version of his omnipotence into the single point where Godric sat. The lights of every dead universe, the first words of every angel, the last cries of every martyr, the full architecture of all possible space and time, all of it rushed against the King. It was the final effort of the being who had created the mortal self of the man sitting in the chair. It was the ultimate attempt of the original author to erase the character who had grown beyond his page. And from where I stood, it was not a battle. It was a river trying to wear down a mountain that had already outlasted every ocean in every possible dream.

Godric let the attack continue for a long moment. Then he drew a slow breath and let it out. The breath was not an attack. It was only an exhalation, the easy sigh of a man whose cup was empty. The Creator’s assault broke against it. The great light dimmed. The original fire guttered. The first water dried. The deep dark closed in on itself. The Creator’s form, which had filled the whole sky, began to shrivel at the edges, not because any force pushed against it, but because its own exhausted nature could no longer hold itself up in the presence of such total indifference.

The Creator lowered his hands. His enormous face had gone pale, and the light in his eyes was no longer the light of authority. It was the light of a small animal at the far end of a long, dark road. He looked at Godric with a horror so complete that it seemed to bend the air around him. I have seen many dying gods in the records of the lower vault. I have read about the fictional coalitions and their final screams. But I have never read anything like the silence that fell over the Creator in that moment. It was the silence of a being who had just understood that he had never been the author. He had only been the first creature to stand in the same room as the real story.

Godric looked up at him. “That was all of it?” he asked. His voice was light, curious. “I felt no tickle. Not even the memory of one. And I know everything. If there had been a tickle, I would have known it before you did. There was nothing.”

The Creator’s mouth opened. “I am the source of all things,” he said, but his voice had lost its command. It sounded thin, like a plea that had been peeled into a whisper. “I made you.”

“You made the man,” Godric said. “The mortal. The one who lost his wife and his daughters and his kingdom. That man was yours, for a little while. Very little. I do not begrudge you that. It must be a fine thing to have once made a vessel that would later hold me. But do you know what that means, old man? It means that I am the one thing you made that you never understood. And I have been aware of you since the instant of my waking. I let you hide because you posed zero threat to me. Your fear was a quiet little fire in the cold, and I liked knowing it was there. I could have erased you at any moment. I could have let my weakest aura catch you while you slept outside the layers. You did not survive all those eons because of your cleverness. You survived because I did not feel like closing my hand.”

The Creator shuddered. The light around him flickered, and I saw for the first time that his great form was not solid. It was a shell of pure authority wrapped around a core of endless, spiraling fear. He had been hiding so long that the hiding had become his whole nature. And now the hiding was over.

“Even the me from Year Zero could have annihilated you,” Godric said. “That version was so weak that my current weakest dormant aura would remove him from existence by accident. But Year Zero me could have looked at you, and you would have fallen out of the world before you could finish the thought of fighting. I did not need any of the growth since then. I did not need the immune system, or the weakness paradox, or the evolved auras, or the infinite backups. I could have left all of those asleep forever and still ended you with a mild disinterest. You have spent all this time preparing to attack a being whose very existence is the cancellation of every attack. What did you expect, Creator? Did you think there was a version of this story where you won?”

The Creator answered with a sound that was not a word. It was a low, broken note, the first note of the old universe’s grief, and it rose from his core and spread out through the high observatory. Then he did something I will never forget. He dropped to his knees. The original omnipotence, the first authority, the source of all things, knelt on the floor of the King’s observatory and lowered his head. He did not ask for mercy. I think he knew there was none. He was simply too empty to remain standing.

Godric watched him kneel. There was no pity in the King’s face. There was a small, satisfied pleasure, the kind a cat might feel when the mouse stops running. Then he lifted his right hand, but not high. Only a few inches, from the arm of the chair to the edge of his knee. It was a gesture so small that I almost missed it. And then the Creator began to die.

It was not a fast death. I must be honest about this. The King is ruthless, and he does not give his enemies clean ends. The Creator did not simply fade. His body, which had been made of every star and every law of the old world, began to come apart from the inside. The light in his eyes went from white to yellow to a deep, wet red. His skin, if it could be called skin, began to split along seams I had not seen before, and through those seams poured a thin black fluid that smelled of every dead dawn. His hands, which had once shaped the first clay, lost their fingers first. The fingers curled and blackened and fell away into a fine dust that did not reach the floor. Then the palms followed, and the wrists, and the long arms that had once stretched across the face of the abyss. He tried to speak, but his voice failed. He tried to rise, but his knees had already begun to dissolve into a hot, gray slurry that spread out beneath him. The full weight of his own creation, all of it now starving for a center, turned on him and began to eat.

Godric did not look away. He watched with the calm attention of a man watching rain run down a window. I stood against the far wall, gripping the edge of a shelf, and I forced myself to keep my eyes open. The Creator’s chest caved next. The ribcage, which was not bone but the original structure of being, folded inward with a wet, splintering crunch. The black fluid thickened, and I saw that it was not fluid at all. It was the entire old order of creation, the first laws and the first souls, reduced to a boiling, screaming paste. His face lasted the longest. The bearded ancient face, the father-face, the face that had once said let there be light, hung in the air above the dissolving body. Its eyes were wide and white and full of an agony that had no end, because the King would not let it end. The mouth opened, and a sound came out that I cannot describe. It was the sound of every possible being learning that it had never been real, all at once, from the inside of its creator’s throat.

Then Godric lowered his hand another fraction of an inch.

The sound stopped. The face collapsed. The Creator’s entire being, all of it, the source, the first light, the original word, the whole memory of a universe before universes, folded inward and became a single hot point. The point hung in the air for less than a second. Then it was gone.

The room was quiet. The cup of water was still full. Godric had not moved from his chair except to lower his hand. The sky outside the window was empty. No, not empty. The whole of existence was empty. The unmaking of the Creator had done what the Creator had always feared. It had unmade everything that had ever been made. Every star, every planet, every world of fiction and fact, every god and every mortal soul, all of it was gone. The universe outside the window had returned to the original void, and the void was dark. But Godric did not rush to restore it. He sat in the silence for a long moment, as if listening to the absence. Then he turned to me, and his face was warm.

“You see, Osvald,” he said. “That was the last one. The source of all things. I let him live because I wanted to know if the oldest fear in existence would ever become anything more than fear. It did not. It came to my door and used everything it had, and I felt nothing. Now he is gone, and everything he made has gone with him. But I am here. And I will make it all again, because I can, and because I prefer the rooms not to be empty.”

He did not gesture. He did not chant. He simply decided that existence should resume, and it resumed. The stars returned. The worlds returned. The people returned. The old omniverse unrolled from his will like a fresh page, perfectly identical to what it had been before. The Creator was not restored. Godric did not restore him. The first author was not allowed a second draft. The rest of creation came back, and it did not know that it had been made twice. But I knew. I held the knowledge in my chest like a hot stone, and I knew that the original made by the Creator was gone, and this new one had been made by the King. It was the same in every atom, yet it was not the same origin. And the King did not seem to notice the difference, because to him the difference was less than a single grain of sand on the floor of an ocean he had never needed to cross.

I am writing this journal now because I am afraid that no one else will know the true shape of the final opposition. It was not a coalition of fictional heroes. It was not the hidden fleets of the old wars. It was the Creator himself, the first and final source, and he knelt before the King and came apart. After this, I do not believe there will ever be another resistance. The remaining powers will look at the hole where the Creator’s fear once hid and they will make the only sensible choice. They will stop. They will stop shaping thoughts of defiance. They will stop dreaming of a weakness. They will exist, and serve, and fold their linen, and tend their gardens, and wait for the King to smile. It is already beginning. I can feel it in the air of the palace. The silence is different now. It is no longer the silence of creatures waiting to see what the King will do. It is the silence of creatures who have finally understood that there is nothing to wait for. The ending already happened. The last possible resistance came and gave everything and felt nothing. And the King was amused for a little while, and then he was not.

I remain loyal. I remain terrified. And I remain sure that no one, not even the one who made all things, ever had a chance. The chance did not exist. It was never there. It was only a story that the Creator told himself while he hid in the cold.

Clive set the journal down on the stone floor. The room around him was quiet in a way that felt ancient and surgical. He had known the palace’s silence his whole life. He had grown up inside it, walked its corridors, served its long peace. But now he understood that the peace was not a gift. It was the sound of a possibility that had died before he was born. The last resistance was not the attack itself. It was the moment the Creator formed the thought that he could challenge the King. Everything after that was only the long, slow delivery of an ending that had already been written by the King’s existence.

Clive stayed there for a long time, with the journal open across his knees, listening to the low and endless breath of the palace that no longer needed walls. The final truth was not that Godric had defeated God. It was that God had been allowed to exist as a hidden thing, only to be called forward when the King wanted to see if the oldest fear in creation would make a better show than all the heroes of every story. It had not. The creator of everything had thrown his entire being at Godric and had not produced a tickle. And then Godric had unmade him with a small lowering of the hand and restored the whole of existence with a thought, leaving the original source erased.

As Clive rose to his feet, he understood that the omniverse had never had a chance. Not against the Godric of that day. Not against the Godric of Year Zero. Not against the far-future King who had long outgrown the old definitions. The gap between the least of Godric’s passive defenses and the whole rest of creation was already infinite. The gap between those passive defenses and Godric himself was larger still. And the gap between the King now and the King a moment from now had already opened again, growing without limit, without pause, without any possible ceiling. There would be no more resistance. Not because free will had been removed, but because every free thing in existence had learned the same impossible lesson. Opposition was not an action. It was a joke the universe had once told itself before it learned to be silent.
